Ecology, Ecosystems and Energy Flow
The base of every environment question

Ecology appears in UPSC Prelims almost every year. Questions on food chains, pyramids, keystone species and biomagnification are routine. GS Paper III also uses these ideas. Pollution, climate and biodiversity answers all rest on how an ecosystem works. If energy flow is clear, much of the syllabus becomes easy.
What ecology studies

Ecology is the study of how organisms relate to each other and to their surroundings. The word was coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866. The term ecosystem was coined by A.G. Tansley in 1935. The levels run from organism to population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere. An ecosystem has abiotic parts (light, soil, water) and biotic parts: producers , consumers and decomposers .
Grazing, detritus and the web

A grazing food chain starts with green plants and moves to herbivores and carnivores. A detritus food chain starts with dead matter, eaten by earthworms and fungi. On land, much more energy flows through the detritus chain. Each feeding level is a trophic level . Real ecosystems form a food web with many linked chains. A web is more stable because an animal can switch food if one source fails.
The ten percent law

Sunlight is the only input. Producers capture only a small part of it. Raymond Lindeman (1942) showed that about 10 percent of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. The rest is lost as heat in respiration. So energy flow is one-way . Nutrients cycle, but energy does not. This is also why food chains rarely have more than four or five links.
GPP, NPP and who is most productive

Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total energy fixed by producers. Net primary productivity (NPP) is GPP minus the energy used by plants in respiration. NPP is the food available to consumers. Per unit area, estuaries, coral reefs and tropical rainforests are among the most productive. Open oceans are poor per area but huge in total because they cover so much of Earth.
Numbers, biomass and energy

The pyramid of energy is always upright. Energy cannot increase going up. The pyramid of biomass is inverted in the sea. Tiny phytoplankton have a small standing crop but multiply fast, and they feed a larger mass of zooplankton and fish. The pyramid of numbers can be inverted too: one big tree supports thousands of insects.
Poisons climb the chain

Some substances are not broken down or excreted: DDT, mercury, cadmium. They build up in fat or tissue. This is bioaccumulation . When the concentration rises at each higher trophic level, it is biomagnification . Top predators suffer most. DDT thinned the eggshells of eagles and falcons. Mercury caused Minamata disease in Japan (1956). Cadmium caused Itai-itai disease.
Niche, keystone species and ecotone

Habitat is where an organism lives. Niche is its role: what it eats, where it lives and how it behaves. A keystone species has an effect far larger than its numbers. Robert Paine (1966) showed this with the starfish Pisaster on rocky shores. An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems, such as mangroves between land and sea. It often holds more species. This is the edge effect .
Vultures and the ecosystem service

India’s vultures crashed by over 95 percent in the 1990s. The cause was diclofenac , a painkiller given to cattle. Vultures ate the carcasses and died of kidney failure. Without vultures, carcasses rotted, stray dogs increased and rabies risk rose. India banned veterinary diclofenac in 2006. This is a clean example of how one lost scavenger breaks the detritus link. The Sundarbans, Western Ghats and Chilika are all good examples of linked food webs under stress.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Ecosystem services are the lifeline of human welfare. Discuss with Indian examples.” Structure: define services (provisioning, regulating, cultural, supporting); give Indian cases (mangroves as storm buffers, wetlands as flood sponges, pollinators); name the threat; end with policy (PES, Green Credit). Mains-style: “Why is biomagnification a concern for human health?” Define, give DDT and mercury, link to Indian pesticide use, suggest bans and organic methods. Prelims tip: Energy pyramids are always upright. Biomass pyramids can be inverted only in aquatic systems. Learn who coined each term.
Biogeochemical Cycles and Ecological Succession
Nutrients cycle, energy does not

Plants and animals use the same atoms again and again. These loops are the biogeochemical cycles . UPSC asks about them in Prelims, and they explain pollution problems such as eutrophication, acid rain and fertiliser overuse. Succession explains how bare land turns into forest and why a disturbed ecosystem recovers. Both topics are short, but they carry sure marks.
Gaseous and sedimentary cycles

In a gaseous cycle the main reservoir is the atmosphere or ocean. Carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycles are gaseous. In a sedimentary cycle the reservoir is the Earth’s crust. Phosphorus and sulphur are sedimentary (sulphur has a small gas phase). Cycles move through pools (reservoirs) and fluxes (flows). Humans now change the flows more than nature does.
Fast and slow loops

Plants take in CO2 by photosynthesis. Respiration, decomposition and burning return it. The biggest store is the rocks (limestone and fossil fuels) . Among active stores, the ocean is the largest. Burning fossil fuels moves ancient carbon into the air in a few centuries. That is why CO2 has gone past 420 ppm (as of 2025) from about 280 ppm before industry.
Why free nitrogen is useless to plants

Air is about 78 percent nitrogen, but plants cannot use it directly. Nitrogen fixation converts it. Bacteria such as Rhizobium (in legume roots), Azotobacter and cyanobacteria like Nostoc do this. Lightning also fixes some. Then ammonification makes ammonia from dead matter. Nitrification turns it into nitrite ( Nitrosomonas ) and nitrate ( Nitrobacter ). Denitrification ( Pseudomonas ) returns nitrogen gas to air.
Rock cycles

Phosphorus comes from rock weathering. It has no gas phase. It is often the limiting nutrient in fresh water. Excess phosphate from detergents and fertiliser causes eutrophication : algal bloom, oxygen loss, fish kills. Sulphur enters the air as SO2 from volcanoes and burning coal. It becomes sulphuric acid in acid rain . Plankton also release dimethyl sulphide, which helps form clouds.
From bare rock to forest

Succession is the orderly change of a community over time. Primary succession starts on bare ground with no soil: new lava, rock or a retreating glacier. Pioneers such as lichens come first (a lithosere ). On open water it is a hydrosere . Secondary succession starts where soil survives: after a fire, flood or abandoned farm. It is much faster.
Seral stages

The steps are called seral stages . The final stable community is the climax community . Early on, production exceeds respiration; at climax they roughly balance. Autogenic succession is driven by the community itself. Allogenic succession is driven by outside forces such as climate. Species diversity and soil depth rise with time.
Is there one climax?

Clements (early 20th century) argued for a single climate climax in a region (monoclimax). Later ecologists such as Gleason and Tansley stressed that local soil and chance matter, so many end states are possible. Modern thinking sees ecosystems as shifting, not fixed. This matters for restoration policy: you cannot simply plant any tree and expect the old forest.
Fertiliser, soil and recovery

Over-use of urea has unbalanced India’s nitrogen cycle. The government pushed neem-coated urea (2015), the Soil Health Card (2015) and nano urea to cut waste. Run-off nitrate and phosphate cause algal blooms in lakes. Secondary succession is the basis of natural regeneration in jhum fallows of the North-East and in mine land reclamation. Mangrove colonisation in the Sundarbans is a classic example of succession in a delta.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Discuss the impact of excessive fertiliser use on the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles in India.” Structure: explain both cycles briefly; show the imbalance (eutrophication, groundwater nitrate, N2O emissions); give policy (neem-coated urea, nano urea, soil health card, organic farming). Mains-style: “Distinguish primary and secondary succession with examples.” Prelims tip: Phosphorus has no gaseous phase. Denitrification returns N2 to air. Succession on rock is a lithosere; on water, a hydrosere.
Terrestrial and Aquatic Ecosystems
Biomes and ecosystems link to the map

Prelims often asks you to match a biome with a climate, a plant or an animal. Mains asks about forests, wetlands and coastal systems. This lesson gives the skeleton. Know the main biomes, India’s forest types, forest cover numbers and the zones of lakes and oceans.
A biome is a large ecosystem type

A biome is a major community shaped by climate, mainly temperature and rainfall. The main ones are tundra, taiga (boreal forest), temperate deciduous forest, grassland, savanna, tropical rainforest, desert and Mediterranean scrub. An ecosystem is smaller and can be a pond or a patch of forest. Biomes change with latitude and with altitude.
Quick guide

Tundra: very cold, permafrost, mosses and lichens, reindeer. Taiga: conifers, long winters; the largest land biome by area. Temperate grassland: prairies (N. America), steppes (Eurasia), pampas (Argentina), veldt (S. Africa), downs (Australia). Savanna: grass with scattered trees; Africa’s plains. Tropical rainforest: hot, wet, richest biodiversity. Desert: under 25 cm rain; succulents like cacti.
Types and cover

Champion and Seth (1968) classified India’s forests into 16 major types, with tropical moist deciduous as the largest group in area. As of ISFR 2023 (the latest I could confirm), India’s forest cover is about 21.76 percent of the area and tree cover about 3.41 percent. Total green cover is about 25.17 percent. The India State of Forest Report is released by the Forest Survey of India every two years.
Where the forests are

By area, Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest cover, then Arunachal Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. By percentage of its area, Mizoram, Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar rank highest. The National Forest Policy 1988 aims for one-third of land under forest or tree cover, and two-thirds in hills. India is still below that.
Still and flowing water

Lentic means still water: lakes, ponds. Lotic means flowing water: rivers, streams. A deep lake has three zones. The littoral zone is the shallow edge with rooted plants. The limnetic zone is open water where light reaches. The profundal zone is deep and dark. Lakes age through eutrophication and silting.
Ocean zones

The sea has a lighted photic zone and a dark aphotic zone . The neritic zone is over the continental shelf and holds most fish. Pelagic means open water; benthic means the sea floor. An estuary is where a river meets the sea. Salinity varies and nutrients are rich, so it is a nursery for fish and prawns. Upwelling brings nutrients to the surface and creates rich fisheries, as off Peru.
Forest cover is not forest quality

India’s cover has risen on paper, but experts point out that the count includes plantations, orchards and bamboo. Natural forest and old-growth stands may be shrinking, and open forest is increasing while very dense forest changes slowly. The question is whether we protect ecosystem function or just green area. This is a standard Mains argument.
Special systems

Loktak Lake in Manipur has floating phumdis . Keibul Lamjao is the only floating national park in the world and shelters the sangai (brow-antlered deer). Chilika is Asia’s largest brackish water lagoon. The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove delta. The Western Ghats and Eastern Himalaya are montane forest hotspots. The Thar and Ladakh cold desert are the dry biomes.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What is the difference between forest cover and tree cover? Why is India’s quality of forest a concern?” Structure: definitions (ISFR terms); latest numbers (as of ISFR 2023); concerns (plantations counted, loss of natural forest, diversion for projects); remedies (CAMPA, community management). Prelims tip: Pampas is Argentina, veldt is South Africa, steppe is Eurasia. Loktak’s phumdis are floating biomass. Champion and Seth gave 16 types.
Ecological Pyramids, Keystone Species and Biomagnification
A favourite Prelims cluster

Pyramids, keystone species and biomagnification are asked almost every other year. They are short concepts, so options are tricky and one wrong word costs the mark. They also power Mains answers on pollution (DDT, mercury), invasive species and wildlife management. Learn the exact definitions once and reuse them.
Three kinds of pyramid

Charles Elton (1927) introduced the pyramid idea. There are three kinds. Pyramid of number: counts of organisms. Can be upright or inverted. Pyramid of biomass: dry weight per area. Inverted in the sea. Pyramid of energy: energy per area per time. Always upright, never inverted. Energy is lost as heat at each step, so the energy pyramid cannot flip.
When the pyramid flips

In a tree ecosystem one big tree supports thousands of insects, so the number pyramid is inverted. A parasitic food chain (tree, birds, lice) is also inverted in numbers. In a pond or ocean the producers are tiny phytoplankton that reproduce fast. At any moment their standing biomass is less than that of zooplankton and fish, so the biomass pyramid is inverted. But their energy turnover is huge, so the energy pyramid stays upright.
Small number, big effect

The term comes from Robert Paine (1969), who removed the starfish Pisaster from a rocky shore in Washington. Mussels took over and diversity fell. A keystone species has an effect far larger than its numbers. Examples: sea otters (they control sea urchins and so protect kelp), African elephants, tigers as top predators, and figs in tropical forests. An umbrella species (tiger, elephant) protects many others when its habitat is protected. A flagship species is chosen to raise public support. An indicator species shows habitat health, such as lichens for air quality.
Toxins climbing the chain

Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a substance inside one organism. Biomagnification is its rise in concentration at each higher trophic level. It happens for substances that are persistent and fat-soluble , so they are not excreted. DDT is the classic case. Rachel Carson wrote Silent Spring (1962) on it. DDT thinned the eggshells of eagles and pelicans. Mercury in fish caused Minamata disease in Japan (1956). Cadmium caused Itai-itai disease.
Do not mix these up

Eutrophication is nutrient over-enrichment of water. It is not biomagnification. Ecological efficiency is the share of energy passed up a trophic level, about 10 percent (Lindeman 1942). Gross primary productivity is total energy fixed by producers. Net primary productivity is GPP minus respiration loss. NPP is what is available to consumers. Standing crop is the mass of living matter at a point in time. Standing state is the amount of nutrients in soil.
Is the keystone idea too neat?

Critics say few species are true keystones. A species can be keystone in one place and ordinary in another. Rewilding projects, such as wolves in Yellowstone (1995), are praised for trophic cascades, but scientists still argue about how large the effect was. Conservation money is limited. Protecting umbrella species is efficient, but it may leave small, unattractive endemic species without cover.
Tigers, vultures and diclofenac

The tiger is India's umbrella species, and Project Tiger (1973) protects whole forests with it. The Asian elephant is a keystone seed disperser. The vulture crash is a lesson in chains. Livestock treated with diclofenac left toxic carcasses. White-backed, long-billed and slender-billed vultures fell by over 95 percent in the 1990s. India banned veterinary diclofenac in 2006. Dead cattle rotted, and feral dogs and rabies cases increased. Sundarbans, Chilika and the Ganga show DDT and heavy-metal traces in fish.
Number versus energy

Remember the one-line rule. Number and biomass pyramids can be inverted. The energy pyramid cannot . A grassland has an upright number pyramid. A forest tree has an inverted one. A sea has an inverted biomass pyramid. All three have upright energy pyramids. Questions often give an example and ask which pyramid is inverted. Match the example to the type.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which pyramid is always upright?" (energy). "Who proposed the keystone concept?" (Paine, 1969). "Biomagnification is caused by substances that are persistent and fat-soluble." Mains-style: "How can the loss of a keystone species threaten an ecosystem? Give Indian examples." Structure: define; Paine's starfish; effect on trophic cascade; Indian cases (vultures, elephants, tiger); policy response; conclusion.
Biomes of the World and India's Biogeographic Zones
Maps behind many questions

Biome and zone questions test whether you can place a species or a forest type on a map. They appear in Prelims through "where is it found" questions on savanna, taiga, tundra or the Deccan Peninsula. Mains answers on biodiversity use these zones to explain why India is mega-diverse.
What a biome is

A biome is a large region with similar climate, plants and animals. Rainfall and temperature decide it. The main land biomes are tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, temperate grassland, temperate deciduous forest, taiga (boreal forest), and tundra. Aquatic biomes are freshwater, marine and estuarine. An ecotone is the transition zone between two ecosystems. Its richness, called the edge effect , is higher because species of both sides meet there.
Quick fingerprints

Tropical rainforest: near the equator, over 2,000 mm rain, layered canopy, highest species richness (Amazon, Congo, Indonesia). Savanna: grass with scattered trees, seasonal rain (Africa, Brazilian cerrado, Australia). Taiga: coniferous forest, long cold winters (Russia, Canada). Tundra: treeless, permafrost, mosses and lichens. Also found on mountains as alpine tundra. Grasslands have local names: prairies (North America), steppes (Eurasia), pampas (Argentina), veldt (South Africa), downs (Australia).
Special cases

Hot deserts (Sahara, Thar) have under 250 mm rain. Cold deserts (Gobi, Ladakh) are dry and cold. Desert plants are xerophytes , with thick cuticles and small leaves. Wetlands are the most productive biome for their area, but are being lost fastest. Mangroves are salt-tolerant forests of tidal coasts. Coral reefs are tropical shallow-sea ecosystems, and they host about a quarter of marine species on under one percent of the seabed.
India's ten zones

The Wildlife Institute of India (Rodgers and Panwar, 1988) divided India into 10 biogeographic zones and 25 provinces. Trans-Himalaya (Ladakh, Lahaul-Spiti) Himalaya Desert (Thar and Kutch) Semi-arid Western Ghats Deccan Peninsula Gangetic Plain North-East Coasts Islands The Himalaya zone alone has several provinces, from the north-west to the east. Rodgers and Panwar's scheme was made for planning protected areas, so each zone was meant to have a network of parks.
What each is known for

The Deccan Peninsula is the largest zone. The Western Ghats are part of a hotspot with high endemism. The North-East is the meeting place of Himalayan, Indo-Malayan and Chinese species. The Trans-Himalaya is the home of the snow leopard and Tibetan antelope (chiru). The Islands zone covers Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep. The Semi-arid zone includes Rajasthan's grasslands, where the great Indian bustard lives.
Zones versus administrative thinking

Biogeographic zones cross state lines, but policy is made by states and districts. Protected areas are drawn on administrative maps, so some zones, like the semi-arid grasslands, are poorly covered. Many grasslands are labelled "wasteland" in land records. This gives them little legal protection, though they hold bustards, wolves and blackbuck.
Numbers to remember

India has about 2.4 percent of world land area but roughly 7 to 8 percent of recorded species. It is one of 17 mega-diverse countries . Forest types follow Champion and Seth (1968): 16 major types in India. Biogeographic realms: India lies at the junction of the Palearctic, Indo-Malayan and Afrotropical realms. Wallace's realms (1876) are the base of this idea.
Biomes and climate change

Biomes shift as climate warms. Tundra thaws and releases methane. Treelines climb mountains. Rainforests dry and burn. Coral reefs bleach. These links turn a biome map into a climate question, which UPSC likes. The Arctic tundra stores huge carbon in frozen soil. When permafrost melts, microbes release methane and carbon dioxide, which warms the planet more. India's own alpine meadows in Uttarakhand and Sikkim are also being squeezed upward.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which biome is called the lungs of the planet?" (tropical rainforest is the common answer; the sea phytoplankton also supply oxygen). "Steppes are temperate grasslands of Eurasia." Mains-style: "Why is India called mega-diverse? Name its biogeographic zones." Structure: numbers; ten zones; hotspots; threats; steps taken.
Biodiversity: Levels, Hotspots and Threats
Biodiversity is asked every year

Hotspots, endemic species, invasive plants and the global biodiversity framework come up often in Prelims. Mains uses them in questions on conservation, climate and development. India holds about 2.4 percent of Earth’s land and a much larger share (roughly 7 to 8 percent) of known species. It is one of the megadiverse countries.
Three levels

Genetic diversity : variation within a species, such as thousands of rice varieties. Species diversity : the number and spread of species. Ecosystem diversity : variety of habitats like forests, wetlands and deserts. Whittaker split species diversity into alpha (within a habitat), beta (between habitats) and gamma (across a region).
Where is diversity high?

Diversity rises toward the equator. This is the latitudinal gradient : tropical regions have more stable climate, more energy and a longer evolutionary history. The species-area relationship (Humboldt) says larger areas hold more species. The equation S = CA^Z gives a slope (Z) of about 0.1 to 0.2 on regional scales. This is why habitat fragmentation matters.
The idea

Norman Myers (1988) proposed biodiversity hotspots. Conservation International now uses two tests: at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and at least 70 percent of original habitat lost . There are about 36 hotspots worldwide. They cover a small fraction of land but hold a very large share of endemic plants and vertebrates.
Where they are

Himalaya : the whole range, including Bhutan, Nepal and parts of Tibet. Indo-Burma : North-East India south of the Brahmaputra, plus Myanmar and more. Western Ghats and Sri Lanka : very high endemism. Sundaland : in India, only the Nicobar Islands. Hotspots are defined by Norman Myers' criteria: at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and loss of at least 70 percent of original habitat. The Eastern Himalaya part is rich in orchids and rhododendrons, and the Western Ghats hold many amphibians. India's Indo-Burma portion includes Manipur, Mizoram and Nagaland, and the Nicobar Islands form its Sundaland part.
Why species are lost

Jared Diamond called the main causes the “evil quartet”: habitat loss and fragmentation , overexploitation , alien species invasion and co-extinction . Climate change and pollution are now added. Habitat loss is the top cause. Poaching, the wildlife trade and human-animal conflict add pressure. Habitat loss includes clearing for farms, mines, dams and roads, and also fragmentation, which splits a large habitat into patches too small for wide-ranging animals such as elephants and tigers. Edge effects then make the remaining patches poorer. Co-extinction means a species dies because its partner does, such as a parasite that depends on one host. The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) also named climate change, pollution and overexploitation among the main drivers.
Plants that take over

India’s major invasives include Lantana camara , water hyacinth , Prosopis juliflora , Parthenium and Chromolaena . They crowd out native plants and reduce grazing and water. The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 gave the Centre power to regulate invasive alien species. Control costs are high, and removal programmes in tiger reserves such as Bandipur and Mudumalai are ongoing. Invasives spread through trade, travel and deliberate introduction. Water hyacinth, native to South America, was brought as an ornamental plant and now chokes ponds and lakes, cutting oxygen for fish. Lantana came from tropical America in the colonial period as a garden shrub and now covers large forest areas. Alien species often lack natural predators in the new home, which is why they spread fast. The Convention on Biological Diversity (Article 8h) asks countries to prevent and control them.
Kunming-Montreal, 2022

The Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio, 1992) set the base. In December 2022 at COP15 (Montreal) , nations adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework with 23 targets for 2030. Key targets: protect 30 percent of land and sea by 2030 (“30 by 30”), restore 30 percent of degraded areas, and mobilise about $200 billion a year from all sources. Developed countries are to give $20 billion a year in international finance by 2025 and $30 billion by 2030.
Law and plans

The Biological Diversity Act 2002 set up the National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai, 2003), State Biodiversity Boards and local Biodiversity Management Committees . It covers access and benefit sharing, based on the Nagoya Protocol. The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023 eased rules for AYUSH users and decriminalised some offences. India released an updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan with national targets in line with the Kunming-Montreal framework (as of 2024). CBD COP17 was due in Armenia in late 2026; check its outcome before the exam.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What are biodiversity hotspots? Why is the Western Ghats a hotspot, and what threatens it?” Structure: definition and two criteria; Western Ghats endemism; threats (mining, plantations, tourism, landslides); Gadgil and Kasturirangan reports; remedies. Mains-style: “Invasive alien species are a silent threat to Indian ecosystems. Discuss.” Prelims tip: Remember the two hotspot criteria numbers (1,500 and 70 percent). India’s hotspot in the Nicobar Islands belongs to Sundaland.
In-situ and Ex-situ Conservation: Protected Areas
Prelims favourite

Questions on national parks, biosphere reserves, tiger reserves and World Heritage Sites come almost every year. Mains asks about conflict between people and protected areas. The key is to know which law creates which category. A simple way to remember is by layers: legal categories under the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, then UNESCO designations such as biosphere reserves and World Heritage Sites, then ex-situ centres. Conflict questions often involve relocation of villages, forest rights under the 2006 Act, and human-elephant or human-tiger conflict near reserve borders.
In-situ and ex-situ

In-situ conservation protects species in their natural home. Examples: national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves. Ex-situ conservation protects them outside: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, cryopreservation. In-situ is better for whole ecosystems. Ex-situ is a backup for species on the edge. Examples of ex-situ work include zoos regulated by the Central Zoo Authority, botanical gardens, and the National Gene Bank run by NBPGR in New Delhi. A key tool is captive breeding followed by reintroduction, as with the gharial. In-situ keeps evolution going in the wild, which ex-situ cannot copy. Most experts say the two approaches work best together, with in-situ as the main strategy.
Under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972

National Park : Section 35. Strictest. No grazing or private rights. Wildlife Sanctuary : Section 26A. Some human activity may be allowed. Conservation Reserve (Section 36A) and Community Reserve (Section 36C): added by the 2002 amendment on government land and community/private land. Tiger Reserve : Section 38V, managed by the National Tiger Conservation Authority. The key difference is that in a sanctuary some activities such as grazing may be permitted by the Chief Wildlife Warden, while in a national park none is allowed. Both are notified by the State government. The 2002 amendment added Conservation and Community Reserves so that people's land could be protected without taking away their rights. Tiger reserves have a core (critical tiger habitat) and a buffer where people and wildlife coexist.
Not under the Wildlife Act

The idea comes from UNESCO’s Man and the Biosphere (MAB) programme (1971). India has a national scheme from 1986 and has about 18 reserves. Each reserve has a core zone (strictly protected), a buffer zone (limited use) and a transition zone (people live and farm). Nilgiri (1986) was first. UNESCO recognises 13 Indian reserves (Cold Desert added in 2025) in the world network, including Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, Gulf of Mannar and Khangchendzonga.
How much is protected

As of recent MoEFCC figures, India has over 1,000 protected areas, roughly 100 national parks and over 500 sanctuaries. They cover about 5 percent of India’s land (figures change slightly each year). The target of 30 by 30 includes OECMs : other effective area-based measures such as community-run sites that are not formally protected.
Natural sites in India

India’s natural World Heritage Sites include Kaziranga , Manas , Keoladeo , Sundarbans , Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers , Western Ghats and Great Himalayan National Park . Khangchendzonga is a mixed site. World Heritage status comes from the 1972 UNESCO convention and listing does not by itself change Indian law.
Zoos and gene banks

The Central Zoo Authority (1992) regulates zoos. The National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in Delhi runs the national seed gene bank. The National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources at Karnal holds animal genetic material. Conservation breeding is used for the Great Indian Bustard (a centre at Jaisalmer), the gharial and vultures. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway is the world’s backup.
Fortress conservation or people’s rights?

Critics say removing people from parks creates displacement and hostility. Supporters say core areas need inviolate space for large predators. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises rights and allows Critical Wildlife Habitats . Sacred groves (Meghalaya’s Law Kyntang, Rajasthan’s Orans, Kerala’s Kavu) show that community conservation also works.
Examples to remember

Kaziranga protects the one-horned rhino. Gir holds the Asiatic lion. Keoladeo is a Ramsar and World Heritage bird site. Simlipal and Nilgiri are biosphere reserves. Sundarbans is both a tiger reserve and biosphere reserve. Eco-sensitive zones (ESZ) around parks regulate activity in a buffer, usually up to 10 km unless fixed otherwise.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Distinguish between in-situ and ex-situ conservation. Which is better for India’s biodiversity?” Structure: definitions; examples; strengths and limits of each; they are complementary; policy (CAMPA, community reserves). Mains-style: “Protected areas versus people: how can both be served?” Prelims tip: Biosphere reserves are not under the WPA. Community reserves are on private or community land. National parks allow no grazing.
Biological Diversity Act 2002 and Benefit Sharing
India's law for the CBD

The Biological Diversity Act is the Indian law that puts the Convention on Biological Diversity into practice. Prelims asks about its three-tier structure, the NBA, People's Biodiversity Registers and the 2023 amendment. Mains links it to biopiracy, traditional knowledge and tribal rights. It is a short Act, so exact detail pays.
Aim and structure

The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 aims at conservation, sustainable use and fair sharing of benefits. It created a three-tier body system: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) , Chennai, set up in 2003. Statutory, autonomous. State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) in states. Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) at local-body level. BMCs prepare People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs) , which record local knowledge about species and uses.
Who needs approval

Foreign nationals, NRIs and foreign companies need NBA approval to access biological resources or knowledge in India. Indian citizens and companies must give prior intimation to the State Board for commercial use. Applying for an intellectual property right based on Indian material (for example a patent) needs NBA approval (Section 6). Local communities and vaidyas and hakims are exempt from the approval rules for traditional use. The NBA sets benefit-sharing terms, such as royalty or a share of fees.
Heritage and threatened species

Under Section 37 , a state can notify areas of biodiversity importance as Biological Heritage Sites (BHS) . The first was Nallur Tamarind Grove near Bengaluru (2007). Other examples include Ameenpur Lake in Telangana and Dhinodhar Hills in Gujarat. The Act also lets the Centre notify threatened species and prohibit or regulate their collection. Sections 36 and 38 relate to such species. BMCs may be consulted by the state and get benefit funds, under the Act's rules.
Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023

Parliament passed the amendment in July 2023 . Main changes: Decriminalised many offences, with penalties from Rs 1 lakh up to Rs 50 lakh instead of jail for several breaches. Exempted AYUSH practitioners (codified traditional medicine) and some cultivated medicinal plants from benefit sharing requirements. Required prior intimation from Indian users and gave BMCs a share in benefits. Eased research, patents and bio-survey and use. Critics fear a weakened regime for local communities.
ABS and patents

Biopiracy is taking resources or knowledge without consent. India's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) holds documented formulae in several languages for patent examiners. The Act also ties in with patent rules : a patent for an invention based on Indian biological material must disclose its source in the application. The Patents Act was amended in 2002 for this disclosure requirement.
Protection or red tape?

Industry argues approvals slowed research and pharma, and sees the 2023 changes as modernising. Activists argue the Act's soul, community control over biological resources, was lost. Another issue is that many BMCs exist only on paper, and PBRs are incomplete. A fair summary is that the Act has the right design but weak local capacity, since most BMCs lack funds and trained members.
Communities and benefit sharing

A well-known case is the Kani tribe of Kerala and the drug Jeevani from the plant arogyapacha (*Trichopus zeylanicus*). The Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute licensed the formula, and the Kani Trust received a share of fees and royalties. It is cited as the best Indian ABS example (late 1990s). Other cases: NBA action on neem and basmati disputes, and a case against firms that used Indian resources without approval.
Facts at a glance

Act: 2002. NBA: 2003, Chennai. Three tiers: NBA, SBB, BMC. PBR: record kept by BMC. Heritage Sites: Section 37; first Nallur Tamarind Grove, Bengaluru. Amendment: 2023, decriminalisation and AYUSH exemption. Parent treaty: CBD. Remember the sequence: CBD 1992, Act 2002, NBA 2003, first Heritage Site 2007, Nagoya Protocol 2010, amendment 2023.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "National Biodiversity Authority is located at" (Chennai). "BMCs prepare People's Biodiversity Registers." Mains-style: "How effective is the Biological Diversity Act in preventing biopiracy and ensuring benefit sharing?" Structure: aims; institutions; ABS example (Kani); limits; 2023 amendment; way forward (empower BMCs, TKDL, funds). Quote the Kani and Jeevani case as the model of fair benefit sharing in any ABS answer.
Invasive Alien Species and Human-Wildlife Conflict
Two growing problems

Invasive species are called the second-biggest cause of species loss after habitat destruction. Human-wildlife conflict hits farmers, forest villages and parks in many states. Both appear in Prelims (name the invasive plant) and Mains (causes and solutions). They also show how law, ecology and livelihood meet.
What is invasive

An alien species is outside its natural range. It becomes invasive when it spreads, harms native species and cannot be kept in check. Causes: trade, travel, gardens, cargo ships (ballast water), aquaculture and road building. Invaders often grow fast, lack predators in the new land and outcompete natives. The CBD (Aichi Target 9 and Kunming-Montreal Target 6) asks for control of invasives. An IPBES report (2023) said invasives cost over US$400 billion yearly worldwide.
Indian invaders

Lantana camara: thorny shrub, covers forests from Mudumalai to Corbett. Water hyacinth (*Eichhornia crassipes*): chokes lakes; called the "terror of Bengal". Parthenium (congress grass): allergy and crop loss. Prosopis juliflora: spreads in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu dry lands. Mikania micrantha: the "mile-a-minute" weed in the North-East and Kerala. African catfish and Nile tilapia: harm fish in rivers and lakes. Senna spectabilis has spread in Wayanad forests.
What the law says

The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 added a section letting the Central Government regulate or prohibit import, trade and spread of invasive alien species . The Biological Diversity Act 2002 (Section 38 and rules) and the Plant Quarantine Order also play roles. The IUCN keeps a list of the 100 worst invasive species. The Invasive Species Specialist Group is part of IUCN. Control methods: mechanical removal, chemical sprays and biological control with a natural enemy, which itself can backfire.
Human-wildlife conflict

Conflict means harm to people, crops or livestock by animals, and killing of animals in return. Main species: elephants , tigers, leopards, wild boar, monkeys, nilgai and crocodiles. Causes: forest loss and fragmentation, development in corridors, invasive weeds that reduce forage, crop raiding, and tourism. Peak sites: Odisha, Assam, Kerala, Karnataka, Uttarakhand and the Sundarbans. The Union Government's annual compensation figures for human death by wild animals run to hundreds of lives in some years.
What works

Early warning systems and SMS alerts (Assam, Tamil Nadu). Solar fences , trench barriers and chilli or bee fences. Crop insurance and quick compensation. Rapid response teams and elephant corridors. Habitat restoration , including removing lantana. Translocation and sterilisation as last choices. The MoEFCC issued advisories on human-wildlife conflict in 2021. In Kerala and Uttarakhand, states have declared some species "vermin" for limited culling under Section 62 of the WPA, which is controversial.
Cull or coexist?

Farmers want right to protect their crops and lives. Conservationists warn that culling and open compensation will not solve habitat loss. Some say wild boar and nilgai should be allowed controlled hunting. Others point to Schedule I animals being counted for sentiment and tourism. A balanced answer: tailor measures to species and landscape.
Cases to quote

In 2016 the Centre allowed state-ordered culling of nilgai in Bihar and wild boar in Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh under Section 62 of the WPA. Kerala suffers from wild boar and elephant raids. The Sundarbans see tiger attacks on honey collectors. Lantana removal in Bandipur and Mudumalai is a restoration project with local labour.
Quick facts

Invasive: spreads and harms natives. Key Indian invaders: Lantana, water hyacinth, Parthenium, Prosopis, Mikania. WPA 2022: powers on invasive alien species. Section 62 WPA: vermin declaration. Solutions: early warning, fences, compensation, habitat repair. Also keep in mind that Lantana alone is estimated to cover a large share of India's forest floor, which is why restoration needs weeding at scale.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which is an invasive alien plant in India?" (Lantana, water hyacinth, Parthenium). "The 'terror of Bengal' refers to" (water hyacinth). Mains-style: "Analyse the rising human-wildlife conflict in India and suggest a way forward." Structure: scale; causes; law; examples; short-term fixes; long-term habitat and corridors; community role.
Species Recovery: Cheetah, Bustard, Gharial, Snow Leopard
Projects with dates

UPSC asks which project belongs to which animal, which state, which IUCN status. Current affairs, like the cheetah translocation, push these species into Prelims and Mains. Treat each species as a small card: status, place, project, threat. Status words matter: one word, such as Critically Endangered versus Vulnerable, often decides a Prelims option.
Project Cheetah

The Asiatic cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952 . Under Project Cheetah , eight African cheetahs from Namibia were brought to Kuno National Park , Madhya Pradesh, on 17 September 2022 . Twelve more came from South Africa in February 2023 . Gandhi Sagar sanctuary was prepared as a second site. The African cheetah is a different subspecies from the Asiatic cheetah, which survives only in Iran. IUCN: cheetah is Vulnerable. Early deaths of several animals raised doubts about the site's space and prey.
A bird at the edge

The great Indian bustard (GIB) is Critically Endangered . Most live in Rajasthan (Desert National Park, Jaisalmer), with small groups in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. It is Rajasthan's state bird, Schedule I of the WPA, and was a candidate for India's national bird in the 1960s. Main threat: overhead power lines that cause collisions. In April 2021 the Supreme Court ordered underground cables in priority areas. Breeding centres at Jaisalmer try to raise chicks. The 2024 order eased the strict ruling and set a balance with renewable energy.
River crocodile

The gharial is a fish-eating crocodilian, Critically Endangered . The main breeding population is in the National Chambal Sanctuary (Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh). Project Crocodile began in 1975 to protect gharial, mugger and saltwater crocodile. Threats: sand mining, dams and irrigation canals, fishing nets and river pollution. Chambal also supports the Gangetic dolphin and the red-crowned roof turtle.
Ghost of the mountains

The snow leopard is listed Vulnerable . Its range in India covers Ladakh, Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal. Project Snow Leopard (2009) uses a community model. The SECURE Himalaya project (UNDP-GEF, with MoEFCC) protects high-altitude landscapes. A first national assessment (2019-23) reported about 718 snow leopards (about 477 in Ladakh), a figure to verify before use. Threats: retaliation killing for livestock, mining, climate-driven loss of snow.
Project list

Project Dolphin (2020): Gangetic dolphin (National Aquatic Animal, 2009), Endangered. Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary in Bihar. Project Crocodile: 1975. Vulture Action Plan (2006): ban on diclofenac; breeding at Pinjore (Haryana). Project Hangul: Kashmir stag in Dachigam, Critically Endangered. Sangai: brow-antlered deer at Keibul Lamjao, Manipur, on floating phumdis. Project Elephant, Project Tiger, Project Lion (Asiatic lion in Gir).
Is reintroduction wise?

Critics say India spent large funds on cheetahs while grassland species like the bustard and blackbuck lose range. Supporters say the cheetah is a flagship for restoring open grasslands. Some argue conservation should first shield habitat and then bring species back. The IUCN has rules for translocation: check the cause of loss, habitat fit and community support.
Grasslands and rivers

Many of these species depend on neglected landscapes: grasslands, riverine sandbars and high-altitude meadows. Land records often call them "wasteland". Policy such as a National Grassland Mission or wise wetland use is needed. The Supreme Court has acted on several species, including the GIB. Some ecologists also argue the cheetah project is not a recovery of the Asiatic cheetah, since India lacks that subspecies.
Table to memorise

Cheetah: Kuno, 2022; extinct 1952. GIB: Critically Endangered; Rajasthan; power lines. Gharial: Critically Endangered; Chambal; Project Crocodile 1975. Snow leopard: Vulnerable; SECURE Himalaya. Dolphin: Project Dolphin 2020. Hangul: Dachigam. Add the Great Indian Bustard Project at Jaisalmer and the Vulture Action Plan 2006 as extra rows.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which species is the target of Project Hangul?" (Kashmir stag). "Where is the National Chambal Sanctuary?" Mains-style: "Evaluate India's species recovery programmes, with special reference to the cheetah project." Structure: aim; method; early results; criticisms (space, prey, cost); lessons; alternatives (grassland protection). Quote one criticism and one reform to show balance.
Eco-Sensitive Zones: Rules, Disputes and Cases
A buffer that sparks fights

Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZs) are around protected areas and are a frequent Prelims and Mains theme because they touch courts, farmers and development. The 2022 Supreme Court order on a one-kilometre buffer made them a news topic again. Know what an ESZ is, who notifies it and what is allowed.
What an ESZ is

An Eco-Sensitive Zone (also called Ecologically Fragile Area) is an area around a national park or wildlife sanctuary that works as a shock absorber . It eases the shift from a strictly protected core to areas of heavier use. It is not a legal term in the Wildlife (Protection) Act . The Centre notifies ESZs under Section 3(2)(v) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and Rule 5(1) of the 1986 Rules. The National Wildlife Action Plan 2002-2016 asked for land around PAs to be notified as ESZ.
The 10 km idea and flexibility

In 2002 the Wildlife Conservation Strategy said ESZs should reach up to 10 km around PAs. The MoEFCC guidelines (2011) say the width can vary from site to site, and where sensitive corridors or areas lie beyond 10 km, the ESZ may extend further. A Monitoring Committee and a Zonal Master Plan , prepared by the state, guide land use. Activities are sorted into three groups: Prohibited: commercial mining, sawmills, polluting industries, major hydroelectric projects, use of firewood commercially. Regulated: tree felling, hotels and resorts, new roads, drawing of groundwater. Promoted: rainwater harvesting, organic farming, renewable energy, eco-tourism.
Supreme Court and the 1 km rule

In Goa Foundation v Union of India (2006) the Court directed that ESZ be notified around PAs. On 3 June 2022 , in the T.N. Godavarman case , the Supreme Court ruled that every protected area must have a mandatory ESZ of at least 1 km from its boundary, and that mining is not allowed within the PA . Several states objected that villages and farms would be hit. In April 2023 the Court modified its order: the 1 km rule would not apply where an ESZ was already notified or proposed under earlier guidelines, and the bar on mining within the PA stayed. The Court also gave relief for areas with existing homes and public use.
Other fragile areas

The EPA 1986 has also been used for named regions: Doon Valley (1989). Dahanu taluka , Maharashtra (1991), where an authority (the Dahanu Taluka Environment Protection Authority, 1996) checks projects. Mahabaleshwar-Panchgani (2001) and Matheran (2003). Bhagirathi Eco-Sensitive Zone , Uttarakhand, notified in 2012 , covering about 100 km from Gaumukh to Uttarkashi. It affected small hydropower projects. The Western Ghats ESA proposals (Gadgil 2011 and Kasturirangan 2013) are the largest of such attempts.
Layers from core outward

Think of the zones as rings. The core of a national park has no human use. The sanctuary allows limited activity. The ESZ regulates activity. Beyond lies general land use . ESZs also keep animals from straying into fields by managing land use at the edge, and they reduce noise, dust and light pollution close to the core.
Whose land is it?

Villagers fear bans on building, farming and wells and say they were not consulted. Developers and states say a blanket 1 km is rigid in dense places like Kerala, where thousands of homes lie within 1 km of PAs. Conservation groups say a thin buffer cannot stop encroachment, mining and roads. The ESZ also lacks direct statutory backing in the WPA, so some experts want it added.
Cases and states

Kerala sought relief after the 2022 order as the 1 km rule would touch homes around many sanctuaries, including Wayanad. Goa and Karnataka have long-pending ESZ proposals around PAs. The Rajaji ESZ and the Corbett ESZ affect tourism. The notification process asks for a draft with a 60-day public comment and then final notification.
Fast facts

ESZ: notified under EPA 1986, not WPA. 2011 MoEFCC guidelines: up to 10 km, flexible. 3 June 2022: SC ordered 1 km minimum; April 2023: modified. Bhagirathi ESZ: 2012. Three lists: prohibited, regulated, promoted. Also remember that a Zonal Master Plan and a Monitoring Committee are the working tools of an ESZ.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Eco-Sensitive Zones are notified under which Act?" (EPA 1986). "Which area is a Western Ghats-linked ecologically fragile area?" Mains-style: "Eco-sensitive zones are essential yet controversial. Discuss." Structure: purpose; legal base; court orders; livelihood and development conflict; reform (participatory master plans, flexible width, statutory backing).
National Parks and Sanctuaries in the News
Current affairs meets static

UPSC often builds questions from a park in the news: where it is, what it holds, what the issue is. A static fact (state, species, legal category) plus a news hook is the pattern. This lesson gives the legal base and then recent cases. Check the latest figures as they change, and treat counts as "as of" values.
Park versus sanctuary

Under the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972: sanctuaries are declared under Section 26A (earlier Section 18) and allow some activities like grazing with permission. National parks are declared under Section 35 , with stricter bans on grazing and private rights. Conservation reserves (Section 36A) and community reserves (Section 36C) cover government and community land. Tiger reserves come under Section 38V . India has over 100 national parks and over 500 sanctuaries , covering about 5 percent of land (counts as of recent years).
Development versus forest

The Great Nicobar Island project (about Rs 72,000 crore, with a transshipment port, airport, township and power plant) is a repeated news item. It needs diversion of about 130 sq km of forest and sits near Campbell Bay National Park and the Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve . The area is home to the Shompen , a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, and the Nicobar megapode. The Galathea Bay Wildlife Sanctuary was denotified in 2021 for the port. NGT and Calcutta High Court reviews and Forest Rights Act concerns have been raised.
Panna and the river link

The Ken-Betwa Link Project (agreement in 2021, foundation in December 2024) will divert water from the Ken to the Betwa in Bundelkhand. Part of the Panna Tiger Reserve (Madhya Pradesh) will be submerged, with about a tenth of its area affected as per reports. The reserve is also a UNESCO biosphere reserve (2020). The Supreme Court's Central Empowered Committee flagged the tiger habitat loss. Compensation plans include a new tiger landscape.
Rhinos and lions

Kaziranga (Assam) holds two-thirds of the world's one-horned rhinos. Floods push animals onto NH-715 , so an elevated corridor was approved in 2025 (check the status). Gir (Gujarat) is the only home of the Asiatic lion . The census showed about 674 lions in 2020 and a higher count reported in 2025 (about 891, to be verified). Lions now live outside the park in the Saurashtra region, and Barda sanctuary is seen as a second home. Kuno is a past plan for a second lion site.
Management stories

Kuno National Park (Madhya Pradesh) hosts the cheetah project. Bandipur and Nagarhole are the site of the night-traffic ban on NH-766 (Kerala demand versus Supreme Court). Jim Corbett drew a Supreme Court rebuke in 2024 over tree felling and illegal construction for a tiger safari at Pakhrau . Sariska and Ranthambore saw tiger translocations. The Ratapani sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh was notified as a tiger reserve in recent years.
Development on the edge

Governments say strategic roads, ports and irrigation matter. Conservationists say forest diversion damages the very sites they claim to protect. Compensatory afforestation does not recreate old forest. The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act 2023 has been challenged on the same grounds. A useful frame: avoid, minimise, then compensate. Ask whether the project truly needs this site.
How to prepare these

For each park in the news, note five things: state, legal category, key species, the issue and the law or body involved (NTCA, NBWL, Forest Rights Act, CAMPA). Create a one-line summary. Use the latest Hindu or Indian Express report for numbers, and mark them with the year.
Static anchors

Sanctuary: Section 26A. National Park: Section 35. Tiger reserve: 38V. Kaziranga: Assam, rhino. Gir: lion. Kuno: cheetah. Panna: Ken-Betwa. Great Nicobar: Campbell Bay NP, Shompen. Check each year's newest additions. Keep a notebook page with one line per park: state, category, species, issue. Mark each fact with its year.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Consider the following protected areas and their states." "Which of these is a tiger reserve?" Know pairs like Panna-Madhya Pradesh and Pakke-Arunachal. Mains-style: "Infrastructure projects near protected areas pose a dilemma. Discuss with examples." Structure: legal safeguards; Ken-Betwa and Great Nicobar; court and NBWL role; compensation limits; way forward.
Species in News and the IUCN Red List
Species in news is a Prelims staple

Almost every Prelims paper has a question on a species: its status, habitat or the park where it lives. UPSC picks animals that were in the news. The method is simple: learn the IUCN status, the Schedule and the place. This lesson gives the system and the animals that recur most.
What the IUCN is

The International Union for Conservation of Nature was founded in 1948 and is based in Gland, Switzerland. It is a union of states and NGOs. Its Red List of Threatened Species is the main global record of extinction risk. The Red List is a scientific assessment, not a law. It does not protect a species by itself. Indian protection comes from the Wildlife (Protection) Act and CITES.
The ladder of risk

From worst to best: Extinct (EX) , Extinct in the Wild (EW) , Critically Endangered (CR) , Endangered (EN) , Vulnerable (VU) , Near Threatened (NT) , Least Concern (LC) . Two more: Data Deficient (DD) and Not Evaluated (NE) . Threatened means CR, EN and VU together. Criteria use population decline, range size, population size and extinction probability.
The Red List in 2026

The Red List now covers well over 170,000 species, and roughly 28 percent of those assessed are threatened. The October 2025 update listed about 172,600 species assessed, of which about 48,600 (around 28%) are threatened. Positive news exists. In October 2025 the green turtle was moved from Endangered to Least Concern globally after conservation gains.
Status of Indian flagships

Tiger : Endangered. Asiatic lion : Endangered. Asian elephant : Endangered. Indian rhino : Vulnerable. Snow leopard : Vulnerable. Cheetah : Vulnerable globally. Ganges river dolphin : Endangered. The IUCN Red List is revised through the year, so these statuses can change. The snow leopard was moved from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2017. The Asiatic lion lives only in Gir and its surroundings in Gujarat. The Ganges river dolphin is India's National Aquatic Animal, and the Indian rhino is found mainly in Assam.
The critically endangered list

Great Indian Bustard : Critically Endangered, mainly Rajasthan. Gharial : Critically Endangered, mainly in the Chambal. Pygmy hog : Critically Endangered, Assam. White-rumped, Indian and slender-billed vultures : Critically Endangered. Hangul (Kashmir stag): Critically Endangered, Dachigam. Sangai (brow-antlered deer) is Endangered. A species' status changes with new assessments, so always check the latest IUCN list. Vultures collapsed in the 1990s after cattle were treated with the drug diclofenac, which poisoned birds that fed on carcasses; the veterinary use was banned in 2006. The Great Indian Bustard faces deaths from collisions with power lines. The pygmy hog is bred in captivity at Basistha near Guwahati and released in Assam grasslands.
International trade and migration

CITES (1973, in force 1975) regulates trade. Appendix I bans commercial trade in species threatened with extinction. Appendix II allows controlled trade. Appendix III lists species a country asks others to help protect. CMS (Bonn, 1979) protects migratory species. India hosted CMS COP13 at Gandhinagar in February 2020 (Great Indian Bustard was a theme). The Wildlife Act 2022 now has a schedule for CITES specimens. CITES works through permits: exporting a listed specimen needs a permit from the exporting country's authority. India has been a party since 1976. Under CMS, Appendix I lists migratory species in danger, while Appendix II lists those that need international agreements. Regional agreements and MoUs, such as the Siberian Crane MoU, follow from it. India has been a CMS party since 1983.
Flagships versus the quiet species

Charismatic animals attract funds: tigers, lions, elephants. Plants, insects and amphibians are far more threatened but get little attention. Critics also say the Red List status is global. A species may be Least Concern globally yet be rare in India. Local lists and the national Schedules therefore matter.
How news links to learning

When a species is in the news, ask five things: Red List status, Wildlife Act Schedule, habitat state, threat, and any project (Project Tiger, Project Cheetah, Project Dolphin, Great Indian Bustard recovery). India’s Wildlife Act Schedule I gives the highest protection; the 2022 amendment kept it for the most endangered. The Great Indian Bustard also gained attention in a 2021 Supreme Court case on power lines in its habitat.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What is the role of the IUCN Red List in conservation planning? Mention its limits.” Structure: purpose; categories; how India uses it; limits (global scale, data gaps, not legally binding); conclusion. Mains-style: “Why do species like the Great Indian Bustard survive in the face of development pressure?” Prelims tip: Learn the “CR list”: GIB, gharial, pygmy hog, hangul, three vultures. Remember threatened = CR + EN + VU.
Wildlife Laws and Projects in India
Law plus projects equals half the topic

UPSC asks both: what the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 does, and what each project achieved. Cheetah, tiger, elephant and dolphin projects are in the news every year. This lesson also uses current facts. Numbers change, so the year is marked. Expect the Act in Prelims through its sections, schedules and bodies, and the projects in Mains through a success versus gaps argument. Project Tiger began in 1973, Project Elephant in 1992, and the Gangetic dolphin received a project in later years. Remember to link each project with the nodal agency and the law that gives it legal force.
Core features

The Act came after the 1972 Stockholm conference. It bans hunting (Section 9), creates protected areas, sets up Wildlife Advisory Boards, and gives schedules of protected species. Penalties are in Section 51. India adopted a Constitutional base in 1976 (42nd Amendment): forests and wild animals moved to the Concurrent List (Entries 17A and 17B), and Article 48A and 51A(g) were added. The Act created schedules of species. Schedule I and Part II of Schedule II carry the highest protection and heaviest penalties. After the 2022 amendment the Act has four schedules, with a new one for CITES-listed specimens, and the old vermin schedule was dropped. The Chief Wildlife Warden is the key State official. The National Board for Wildlife, chaired by the Prime Minister, advises the Centre.
What changed (in force 2023)

The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 did these things: it cut the schedules from six to four; it dropped the vermin schedule; it added a schedule for CITES specimens and made the Centre the CITES authority; it gave power to regulate invasive alien species ; and it allowed states to reconstitute their Wildlife Advisory Board as a Standing Committee. It also allows voluntary surrender of captive wild animals and regulates elephant transfer for religious uses.
Gaps and concerns

Critics say the Amendment shifts power to the Centre and weakens oversight of captive elephants. Supporters say it brings India in line with CITES and helps curb invasives. Enforcement is weaker than the law. The Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (2007) tackles trade, but conviction rates are low.
The model

Project Tiger began in 1973 (Corbett was first). The National Tiger Conservation Authority became statutory in 2006. The 2022 estimate reported at least 3,167 tigers from camera traps and a mean estimate near 3,682 , which is about 70 percent of the world’s wild tigers. The next estimation (sixth cycle) began in 2025–26 and its report is expected in 2027. India has 58 tiger reserves in 18 states (as of 2026).
As of 2026

The cheetah went extinct in India in 1952. Eight Namibian cheetahs were released at Kuno National Park (Madhya Pradesh) on 17 September 2022. Twelve more came from South Africa in 2023. Cubs are now born in India. As of September 2026, secondary reports count about 52 cheetahs , including around 32 born in India, with a few at Gandhi Sagar sanctuary. Banni (Gujarat) and other sites are being prepared. Botswana is a new source country.
Quick table

Project Elephant (1992): corridors and elephant reserves. The 2017 census counted 27,312 elephants. The DNA-based 2021–25 estimate, released in October 2025, counted about 22,446 elephants; it uses a new method, so it is not directly comparable. Project Snow Leopard (2009) and the SECURE Himalaya programme. Project Dolphin (announced 2020) for river and ocean dolphins. Crocodile Conservation Project (1975) and gharial work in the Chambal. Project Lion for Gujarat’s Asiatic lions; the 16th lion census (May 2025) counted 891, up from 674 in 2020.
Is translocation worth it?

Cheetah supporters say it restores a grassland predator and funds grasslands. Critics say India lacks enough open space, deaths were high in early years, and money would be better spent on the Great Indian Bustard or caracal. The Supreme Court monitored the project and asked for more sites. The same question applies to tiger relocation: how many animals can the land hold?
Related laws

Related laws: Forest Conservation Act 1980 (now renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam after the 2023 amendment), Forest Rights Act 2006 , Biological Diversity Act 2002 and the Environment Protection Act 1986 . The Supreme Court’s M.K. Ranjitsinh v Union of India (2024) case, on the Great Indian Bustard, recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Evaluate the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022. Does it strengthen conservation?” Structure: key changes; positives (CITES, invasives, rationalised schedules); negatives (centralisation, captive animals, enforcement); way forward. Mains-style: “Project Cheetah: success or experiment? Discuss.” Prelims tip: The 2022 Act cut schedules from six to four. Kuno is in Madhya Pradesh. NTCA is statutory since 2006.
Biodiversity Hotspots and Mega-diverse Countries
A Prelims regular

Hotspot questions appear again and again: how many are in India, which hotspot covers which state, and what the criteria are. Mains also asks whether hotspot thinking helps or hurts conservation. Know the criteria, the four Indian hotspots and what each one holds. A frequent trap: the Eastern Ghats and the Western Ghats are often swapped in options.
Myers and the two criteria

The idea was proposed by Norman Myers in 1988. Conservation International later adopted and refined it. A region is a hotspot if it: has at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species (over 0.5 percent of the world total); and has lost at least 70 percent of its original natural vegetation. World total is 36 hotspots (as of the 2016 update). They cover about 2.5 percent of land but hold over half of the world's endemic plants.
The four hotspots

India has four hotspots, partly or wholly inside its borders. Himalaya: the Himalayan arc across Bhutan, Nepal and north India. Indo-Burma: includes north-east India (outside the Himalaya) and Myanmar, Thailand and others. Western Ghats and Sri Lanka: the Western Ghats were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012. Sundaland: includes the Nicobar Islands. The Eastern Ghats are not a hotspot.
Endemics and flagship species

The Western Ghats are home to the lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr and Malabar civet. The Himalaya holds the red panda, snow leopard and Himalayan monal. Indo-Burma has the hoolock gibbon (India's only ape) and many orchids. The Nicobars have the Nicobar megapode and giant robber crab. Endemism is the key. A species found only in one area, and lost there, is lost to the world.
Another list

The 17 mega-diverse countries were named by Conservation International and UNEP-WCMC (1998). They hold about 70 percent of world biodiversity. India is one. Others include Brazil, Indonesia, Colombia, China, Australia, Mexico and South Africa. A country can be mega-diverse without being a hotspot, and a hotspot can cross many countries. Do not confuse the two.
Beyond hotspots

Other ways to rank conservation areas: Global 200 ecoregions (WWF). Endemic Bird Areas (BirdLife). Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs). India has over 500. Key Biodiversity Areas. Frontier forests and high-biodiversity wilderness areas. Hotspots focus on threat plus endemism. Wilderness areas focus on intact, low-threat regions.
Do hotspots serve conservation?

Supporters say hotspots give clear priorities and attract funding, such as the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund. Critics say they ignore vast low-endemism ecosystems like savannas, ignore animals, and may neglect the poor who live inside them. A few say the 70 percent loss test rewards areas that are already damaged. A balanced answer: hotspots are a triage tool, not a full strategy.
Threats and responses

Threats include dams, mining, monoculture plantations, shifting cultivation in the North-East, and tourism pressure. The Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel (Gadgil, 2011) and the High-Level Working Group (Kasturirangan, 2013) debated how much to protect. Responses: protected areas, biosphere reserves such as Nilgiri and Nokrek, and the Biological Diversity Act 2002. Climate change adds new pressure on mountain species.
Numbers to hold

Criteria: 1,500 endemic plants, 70 percent loss. World hotspots: 36. India: 4 (Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Sundaland). Mega-diverse countries: 17. If a question gives a species and asks for its hotspot, think of its habitat first. The hoolock gibbon points to Indo-Burma.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Consider the following statements on biodiversity hotspots" with the two criteria. Remember that endemism and habitat loss are both needed. Mains-style: "What are biodiversity hotspots? Discuss the conservation challenges of India's hotspots." Structure: define; criteria; four Indian hotspots; threats; policy; way forward. Remember also that hotspots are about plants and endemism, so a hotspot does not automatically have the most animals or the most forest cover.
Biosphere Reserves in India and the MAB Programme
Often mixed with parks

Biosphere reserves are a Prelims favourite because the statements mix them with national parks and sanctuaries. The big difference: biosphere reserves are not created by the Wildlife (Protection) Act. They are a UNESCO idea carried out through the central government. Learn the zones, the list and the first one.
The MAB Programme

UNESCO launched the Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme in 1971. The World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR) began in 1976. Sites stay under national law and are nominated by countries. An Indian biosphere reserve is declared by the central government on the scheme Biosphere Reserve Programme , run by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). It tries to join conservation with use by local people.
Core, buffer, transition

Each reserve is arranged in three zones. Core: legally protected, minimal human activity, undisturbed. Buffer: surrounds the core; research, education and limited use allowed. Transition: outer area where people live and farm, working with managers. Three functions: conservation , development (sustainable) and logistic support (research and monitoring).
India's list

India's first biosphere reserve was the Nilgiri (1986), spanning Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka. India has 18 biosphere reserves designated by the government. Examples: Nanda Devi (Uttarakhand), Khangchendzonga (Sikkim), Nokrek (Meghalaya) Sundarbans (West Bengal), Gulf of Mannar (Tamil Nadu) Great Nicobar, Simlipal (Odisha), Pachmarhi (Madhya Pradesh) Achanakmar-Amarkantak, Agasthyamala, Panna, Dibru-Saikhowa, Dihang-Dibang The UNESCO network includes about twelve of these (as of 2020; check the latest).
What to remember

Gulf of Mannar was the first marine biosphere reserve in South Asia. Sundarbans is a mangrove and tiger landscape, also a Ramsar site and World Heritage Site. Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers are a World Heritage Site together. Panna (2020) was among the recent UNESCO additions. Check whether a name asked in an exam is in the UNESCO list or only the Indian list.
How they differ

A national park has fixed legal boundaries and bans grazing and private rights. A biosphere reserve is larger, has zones, and may include national parks and sanctuaries inside. A conservation reserve and community reserve are WPA categories on government and community land. So a biosphere reserve is a planning layer. The legal teeth come from the park or sanctuary inside it.
Paper reserves?

Critics say biosphere reserves lack a dedicated law, so rules in buffer and transition zones are weak. Local people may not gain from them. Funding is thin, and boundaries are often drawn without community consent. Supporters argue they are the only model that accepts people living in a landscape, which fits India.
Why this suits India

Many Indian reserves are home to forest communities. Tribal groups in Nilgiri (Todas, Kotas) and Nokrek (Garo) depend on resources there. The Forest Rights Act 2006 and joint forest management link to biosphere zones. In Sundarbans, mangrove fishing and honey collection need regulated use. The Nilgiri reserve also protects the Silent Valley and Mukurthi areas, and holds the Nilgiri tahr and the lion-tailed macaque.
Quick facts

MAB launched: 1971. First Indian reserve: Nilgiri, 1986. Zones: core, buffer, transition. Not created by the Wildlife (Protection) Act. Nodal ministry: MoEFCC. Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, Gulf of Mannar and Nilgiri are the most asked names. A good habit is to link each reserve with its state and its flagship species before the exam.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which of the following are biosphere reserves?" Check Nokrek, Simlipal, Pachmarhi. Remember that Kanha is a tiger reserve and national park, not a biosphere reserve. Mains-style: "How are biosphere reserves different from national parks? Do they help both conservation and people?" Structure: definition; zones; difference; examples; limits; reform.
Tiger Reserves, Project Tiger and the Tiger Census
India's flagship species

The tiger is a favourite of both Prelims and Mains. Questions ask for the launch year of Project Tiger, the NTCA's status, census numbers, and zones inside a reserve. It is also the best example of an umbrella species policy. Watch the dates: the Act is 1972, the project is 1973, and the statutory NTCA is 2006.
Project Tiger

Project Tiger was launched on 1 April 1973 with nine reserves, starting with Jim Corbett . It followed a fall in tiger numbers to about 1,800 in the early 1970s. It is a centrally sponsored scheme, now under the MoEFCC. The Wildlife (Protection) Act was amended in 2006 to create the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) as a statutory body. The same amendment set up the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (2007) to fight poaching and trade.
Core and buffer

Under Section 38V of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, a tiger reserve has: Core or critical tiger habitat: legally inviolate, no human activity, declared by the state with expert advice. Buffer or peripheral area: a mixed-use area for co-existence. Village relocation from the core must be voluntary and with a package, as the Forest Rights Act 2006 requires. Critical tiger habitats are to be notified after consulting local gram sabhas.
How tigers are counted

The All India Tiger Estimation is done every four years, run by the NTCA with the Wildlife Institute of India. It uses camera traps and capture-recapture statistics, not just pugmark counts. 2006: 1,411 2010: 1,706 2014: 2,226 2018: 2,967 2022: 3,682 (camera-trap estimate, announced in April 2023) India holds about 75 percent of the world's wild tigers. Madhya Pradesh has the largest number.
Examples to know

Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand): oldest, 1936 as Hailey National Park. Sundarbans (West Bengal): the only mangrove tiger habitat. Ranthambore (Rajasthan) , Bandhavgarh and Kanha (Madhya Pradesh) . Periyar (Kerala) , Bandipur (Karnataka) , Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam (Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, the largest by area) . Pakke and Namdapha in Arunachal Pradesh. India has well over 50 tiger reserves.
International links

The tiger range countries signed the St. Petersburg Declaration (2010) with the goal TX2, to double wild tigers by 2022. The Global Tiger Forum is an inter-governmental body based in New Delhi. The International Big Cat Alliance was launched in April 2023 at Mysuru for seven big cats, led by India. The tiger is Endangered on the IUCN Red List and Schedule I of the WPA.
Tigers and people

Rising numbers cause conflict in the buffer zone. Reserve boundaries are full, so tigers move out of the parks. Relocating villages is slow and costly. Critics say the model is "fortress conservation". Supporters point to the rise from about 1,400 to over 3,600 in two decades and to better prey and water protection.
Corridors and linear projects

Tigers need corridors. Roads, railways and canals cut them. The Kanha-Pench corridor and Terai Arc are key. The Supreme Court and the NTCA have issued guidance on eco-sensitive zones. The NTCA also runs the M-STrIPES monitoring app. Wildlife crime remains a risk with poaching for skins and bones.
Fast facts

Project Tiger: 1973, Corbett first. NTCA: statutory from 2006. Core: critical tiger habitat; buffer around it. Census: every four years; 3,682 in 2022. Tiger Day: 29 July (International Tiger Day). Global Tiger Day was set at the 2010 St. Petersburg summit. India reported its numbers at Mysuru in April 2023, when Project Tiger completed 50 years.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Project Tiger was launched in:" (1973). "Which Act provides for tiger reserves?" (WPA 1972 amended 2006). Mains-style: "Examine the success of Project Tiger. What new challenges does it face?" Structure: launch; numbers; legal base; successes; conflicts, corridors, relocation; way forward. Use numbers sparingly but exactly: 1,411 to 3,682 across 2006 to 2022 is a strong line in a conclusion.
Elephants, Rhinos and Their Conservation Projects
Projects and pachyderms

UPSC likes species projects: which year, which animal, which state. Elephant and rhino are also common in current affairs because of human-wildlife conflict and poaching. This lesson gives the key dates and numbers. Expect questions that link species with their status on the IUCN list and with the right Schedule of the WPA.
Project Elephant

Project Elephant was launched in 1992 to protect elephants, their habitat and corridors, and to address conflict. It is run by the MoEFCC. India has about 33 elephant reserves in over 14 states. The Asian elephant is Endangered (IUCN) and in Schedule I of the WPA. The Government declared the elephant a National Heritage Animal in 2010 , after the Elephant Task Force (2010) report Gajah . World Elephant Day is 12 August.
Where they live

The 2017 census counted about 27,312 elephants. Karnataka had the most, followed by Assam and Kerala. A later DNA-based count in 2025 reported a lower figure (verify before using). India holds over half of all wild Asian elephants. Habitat patches are shrinking. Over 400 people a year are killed in conflict across India (government figures, recent years), and elephants die from train hits, electric fences and poisoning. Rail corridors in Assam and Odisha are black spots.
Moving between forests

An elephant corridor is a strip of land that links two forests. India has over 100 identified corridors. Wildlife Trust of India and the MoEFCC published a report on them. Some are on private land, so their protection needs state action. Underpasses and speed limits on trains help. A mother herd roams hundreds of square kilometres.
Greater one-horned rhino

The Indian rhino is Vulnerable (IUCN) and Schedule I. It is found mostly in Kaziranga (Assam), also in Pobitora, Orang and Manas, and in Jaldapara and Gorumara in West Bengal. Kaziranga is a World Heritage Site (1985). The population in India is about 4,000, over 2,600 in Assam. The Indian Rhino Vision 2020 was a plan from 2005 to reach 3,000 rhinos in Assam by translocation. Poaching for horn is the main threat. Rhinos are also flood-prone.
Javan and Sumatran

The Javan rhino (Critically Endangered) lives only in Ujung Kulon in Indonesia. The Sumatran rhino is also Critically Endangered. The white and black rhinos are African. Two African rhino species are mixed up in questions with the Indian one. The Asian rhinos have one or two horns; African rhinos have two.
Poaching or habitat?

Ivory and horn trade is still a threat, but the larger long-term threat is habitat loss. Compensation and conflict are huge. Some states allow chilli fences, bee fences and early-warning SMS. Critics say translocation of "problem" elephants to captivity or zoos is cruel. Temples and mahouts raise the issue of captive elephants.
Policy tools

The Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 bans hunting and trade. Project Elephant and the Elephant reserve model are administrative. The Supreme Court (2020) upheld the Nilgiris elephant corridor near Mudumalai. Karnataka and Kerala have railways limiting speeds on elephant tracks. The MIKE programme (Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants) is a CITES tool.
Numbers

Project Elephant: 1992. Heritage Animal: 2010. Elephant reserves: about 33. Census 2017: 27,312. Rhino: Kaziranga, Vulnerable. World Elephant Day: 12 Aug. Tiger, elephant, rhino, lion and leopard are all Schedule I species. Their reserves and census cycles are often paired in one question. The 2017 census total of 27,312 is the figure most questions use.
How to answer
