Prelims-style: "Project Elephant was launched in" (1992). "Which state holds the highest elephant population?" (Karnataka in 2017). Mains-style: "Why is human-elephant conflict rising and what can be done?" Structure: causes (habitat loss, corridors, crop raids); impact; policy (Project Elephant, corridors); local solutions; way forward. Add one local solution, such as early-warning systems in Assam or honey-bee fences in Karnataka, to lift a Mains answer. A Prelims favourite is the pairing of project and year, so write each pair down.
The Convention on Biological Diversity and Its Protocols
The treaty behind the law

The CBD is the base of India's Biological Diversity Act 2002 and of global talks on nature. Prelims asks about its protocols (Cartagena, Nagoya), its targets (Aichi, Kunming-Montreal) and which body administers it. Mains asks how India aligns national law with it. Also remember that the treaty has no binding targets of its own; the targets come from decisions at each COP.
Three goals

The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit (1992) and entered into force in 1993 . India became a party in 1994. It has three objectives: Conservation of biological diversity. Sustainable use of its components. Fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources. The Secretariat is in Montreal . The COP is its decision body. The United States signed but did not ratify.
Cartagena and Nagoya

Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000, in force 2003): governs safe handling and trade of living modified organisms (LMOs). Uses the advance informed agreement procedure. Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing (2010, in force 2014): sets rules for access to genetic resources and traditional knowledge and sharing of benefits. Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol (2010): liability and redress for damage from LMOs. India is a party to all three.
Aichi to Kunming-Montreal

The Aichi Biodiversity Targets (20 targets for 2011 to 2020) were adopted at COP10 in Nagoya, Japan (2010). Most were missed. At COP15 (Montreal, December 2022) countries adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework with 23 targets for 2030 . Key goals: 30 by 30: protect 30 percent of land, inland water, coasts and oceans by 2030. Restore 30 percent of degraded ecosystems. Mobilise at least US$200 billion a year from all sources by 2030, and cut harmful subsidies by $500 billion a year.
Who supports the CBD

IPBES (2012) is the science panel, like the IPCC for nature. GEF is the financial mechanism. IUCN Red List tracks species status. TEEB (2007-10) put values on ecosystem services. COP16 was held in Cali, Colombia (2024). Check the latest COP for exams. The Global Environment Facility channels funds, and a new Global Biodiversity Framework Fund was set up under it in 2023.
Access and benefit sharing

Genetic resources are material with real or potential value. ABS means a user, such as a company, must get prior informed consent and agree mutually-set terms with the provider country. Bioprospecting is searching nature for valuable products. Biopiracy is use without consent or sharing. Famous cases: neem, turmeric and basmati patent disputes, where India challenged patents at the European and US offices. The turmeric patent was revoked in 1997 and the neem patent by the EPO (final decision 2005).
Does it work?

The CBD has no strong enforcement and the US is not a party. Rich countries want access to genes at low cost; poor countries want funds and technology. Digital sequence information (DSI) is a new fight: gene data online is used without sharing benefits. COP16 began a fund for DSI sharing. Some say a legally binding target regime, like the Paris Agreement, is needed.
National implementation

India implements the CBD through the Biological Diversity Act 2002 , the National Biodiversity Authority in Chennai and state boards. India has a National Biodiversity Action Plan and a NBSAP update. The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) blocks wrong patents on Ayurveda and Yoga. India hosted COP11 of the CBD at Hyderabad in 2012, where it launched the Hyderabad Pledge on funds.
Dates in one place

CBD: 1992 signed, 1993 in force. Cartagena: 2000. Nagoya: 2010. Aichi: 2010 for 2011-20. Kunming-Montreal: 2022 with 23 targets and 30 by 30. COP11: Hyderabad 2012. Secretariat: Montreal. India also announced a revised NBSAP aligned to the 2030 targets, and the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023 came after the Montreal deal.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which protocol deals with LMOs?" (Cartagena). "Nagoya Protocol relates to access and benefit sharing." Mains-style: "Discuss the importance of the Kunming-Montreal Framework for India." Structure: targets; 30 by 30; finance; India's laws and NBSAP; challenges (people, funds); way forward. A sharp conclusion links the 30 by 30 target to India's existing protected area share of roughly five percent of land.
CITES, CMS and Other Wildlife Conventions
Treaties on animals

Prelims often asks which treaty does what: trade, migratory species, wetlands or whaling. Many questions give a species and ask which Appendix or convention applies. A clean table in your head removes most confusion. Keep a three-line table: CITES for trade, CMS for migration, Ramsar for wetlands. Most wrong options swap these.
Trade in endangered species

The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora was signed at Washington in 1973 and came into force in 1975 . India joined in 1976. The secretariat is in Geneva, hosted by UNEP. CITES works through permits , not outright bans on all trade. Appendix I: threatened with extinction; trade almost banned (tiger, rhino, Asian elephant). Appendix II: trade regulated; may become threatened. Appendix III: a country asks others to help control trade in a species.
Migratory species

The Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals , also the Bonn Convention , was adopted in 1979 (in force 1983). India is a party. It has Appendix I (endangered migratory species with strict protection) and Appendix II (species needing international cooperation). Agreements under CMS: the Siberian Crane MoU (1998, India signed), the Dugong MoU, the Raptors MoU and the Marine Turtles MoU. India hosted CMS COP13 at Gandhinagar in February 2020 , with the great Indian bustard as its mascot.
A summary table

Ramsar (1971): wetlands of international importance. World Heritage (1972): natural and cultural sites. IWC (1946): whaling; moratorium on commercial whaling from 1986. India is a member and is against whaling. UNCLOS (1982): the law of the sea. Bern, Lusaka and Lusaka Agreement: regional. Convention on Wetlands, CMS, CITES and World Heritage together make the "biodiversity cluster".
Implementation

CITES is applied in India through the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 , and through the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act and Customs rules. The 2022 amendment to the WPA gave legal basis for CITES permits and a Management Authority. The Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (2007) tracks trade in tiger bone, rhino horn, pangolin scales and star tortoises. India has proposed or supported moves to keep some species, such as the Indian star tortoise, at Appendix I.
Appendix examples

Appendix I: tiger, leopards, snow leopard, Asian elephant, Indian rhino, red panda. Appendix II: most orchids, some sharks. The Indian star tortoise was moved to Appendix I in 2019. Pangolin species were moved to Appendix I in 2016. Ivory trade bans date from 1989. Movements between appendices are decided at the CITES COP, held every three years.
Ban or regulate?

Some say legal markets (for example, in ivory) fund conservation. Others say they cover illegal trade. India opposes legal trade in ivory. Community-based harvest, such as for vicuna wool, is cited as proof that regulated trade can help. CITES has weak punishment for violators and is not designed to protect habitats.
Migration and wetlands

India lies on the Central Asian Flyway , used by birds such as the bar-headed goose and Amur falcon. The Amur falcon at Doyang reservoir (Nagaland) is a conservation story: hunting was banned and now the village is a tourism site. Chilika, Keoladeo and Pong Dam host migratory birds.
Years to hold

CITES: 1973 signed, 1975 in force. India 1976. CMS: 1979. India hosted COP13, 2020. Ramsar: 1971. World Heritage: 1972. IWC: 1946; moratorium 1986. CITES COPs meet roughly every three years; the CMS COP meets every three years too, and its Scientific Council advises it. A Prelims favourite is the Appendix system, so memorise what I, II and III mean.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which convention regulates international trade in endangered species?" (CITES). "Which treaty protects migratory animals across borders?" (CMS). Mains-style: "Examine how international conventions help India protect wildlife." Structure: CITES and CMS role; Ramsar and WHC; WPA link; wildlife crime; limits; way forward. Use one Indian example per convention: tiger bone under CITES, Amur falcon under CMS, Chilika under Ramsar.
Air Pollution and Air Quality
Winter smog is a yearly headline

Every winter Delhi and the Indo-Gangetic Plain choke on smog. UPSC asks about the Air Act, AQI, NCAP, BS-VI, stubble burning and health. Mains wants causes, policy and a way forward. The numbers below matter in Prelims. The causes and policy gaps matter in Mains.
Primary and secondary pollutants

Primary pollutants are released directly: SO2, NOx, CO, particles. Secondary pollutants form in the air: ground-level ozone and PAN. PM2.5 and PM10 are particles under 2.5 and 10 micrometres. PM2.5 enters the lungs and blood and causes the most harm. Other pollutants: lead, ammonia, benzene, benzo(a)pyrene, arsenic, nickel.
Two kinds

Photochemical smog (Los Angeles type) needs sunlight, NOx and volatile organic compounds. It makes ozone and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN). Classical or sulphurous smog (London 1952) comes from coal smoke and SO2 in cold, humid air. The Great Smog of 1952 led to the UK Clean Air Act 1956. Delhi’s winter smog combines both with temperature inversion.
NAAQS and AQI

India’s National Ambient Air Quality Standards (2009) cover 12 pollutants. The annual limit for PM2.5 is 40 µg/m3 and the 24-hour limit is 60. For PM10 they are 60 and 100. The National Air Quality Index was launched in 2014 with six bands: Good, Satisfactory, Moderate, Poor, Very Poor and Severe. The WHO guideline (2021) is much tighter: 5 µg/m3 annual for PM2.5.
Air Act 1981 and the rest

The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981 follows the Stockholm conference. It set up the CPCB and State Boards and allowed air pollution control areas. The Environment Protection Act 1986 provides the umbrella rules. For Delhi NCR, the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) was set up in 2020 and given statutory form in 2021. The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) imposes steps as AQI worsens.
Policy tools

The National Clean Air Programme (January 2019) targets about 130 non-attainment cities. It began with a 20 to 30 percent cut in PM goal by 2024 against 2017, later revised to 40 percent by 2025–26. Money flows through the PRANA portal and the 15th Finance Commission’s performance grants. Bharat Stage VI fuel and engine norms started in April 2020, skipping BS-V. Other steps: Ujjwala LPG, power plant FGD rules, EV push (PM E-DRIVE), and subsidies for crop residue machines.
Who pollutes

Main sources are vehicles, road dust, construction, coal power plants, industry, biomass cooking and crop-residue burning in Punjab and Haryana in October-November. Studies differ on shares because meteorology varies. Transport and dust dominate in Delhi on most days; stubble contributes a large spike in some weeks. Indoor air from solid-fuel cooking remains a major rural killer.
Quick fixes or deep fixes?

Odd-even schemes, smog towers and cloud seeding trials give visible action but little evidence of big impact. Critics say the airshed approach across states is the real need, with enforcement on industry, transport and power. Another debate: tighten standards to WHO levels or make them achievable first? A third: is air quality a health emergency or a development trade-off?
Beyond Delhi

Many studies rank cities in the Indo-Gangetic Plain and parts of the North-East among the most polluted in the world. The health burden includes asthma, COPD and early deaths. The Sustainable Development Goals and the Right to Life (Article 21) frame clean air as a right. Courts have repeatedly directed Delhi on vehicles, fuel and construction dust (M.C. Mehta cases).
How to answer

Mains-style: “Why does northern India suffer from severe air pollution every winter? Suggest measures.” Structure: causes (inversion, stubble, vehicles, dust); health and economic cost; current measures (NCAP, GRAP, CAQM, BS-VI); gaps; airshed approach, crop diversification, public transport. Prelims tip: Learn six AQI bands, the NAAQS year (2009), NCAP (2019) and BS-VI (2020). Air Act is 1981; Water Act is 1974.
Water, Soil and Noise Pollution
Everyday pollution, regular questions

Rivers, groundwater and noise are classic GS-III topics. Prelims tests terms like BOD and COD. Mains asks for causes, laws and schemes like Namami Gange. One idea ties everything: pollution is not only about industry. Sewage and farming matter most in India. Water, soil and noise pollution are linked: fertilisers and pesticides from soil wash into rivers, and untreated sewage reaches groundwater. Also remember that rural India faces chemical contamination of groundwater, while cities face sewage and traffic noise. Link each type to its law and its monitoring agency, and always add a named scheme.
Indicators

Dissolved oxygen (DO) must be high for aquatic life. BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) shows organic pollution: high BOD means low DO. COD (chemical oxygen demand) includes chemically oxidisable matter and is higher than BOD. Eutrophication from nutrients causes algal bloom and fish kills. India’s biggest source is untreated sewage. CPCB's criteria for bathing water ask for DO of 5 mg/l or more and BOD of 3 mg/l or less. Other indicators are the faecal coliform count, which shows sewage contamination, plus pH, turbidity and total dissolved solids. Bioindicators help too: some insect larvae such as stoneflies live only in clean water, while sludge worms survive in polluted water.
Natural and man-made problems

Fluoride above 1.5 mg/L causes fluorosis (Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh). Arsenic above 0.01 mg/L causes skin and cancer problems (Ganga plains, West Bengal, Bihar). Nitrate rises from fertiliser. Over-extraction also draws up salt and uranium in some areas. The Central Ground Water Board monitors this. Fluorosis damages teeth and bones, and arsenic exposure also causes skin lesions. The WHO guideline value for arsenic is 0.01 mg per litre, which India's drinking water standard follows. Over-extraction is highest in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan, where the water table falls every year. Rainwater harvesting, managed aquifer recharge and the Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019) address this.
What exists

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 set up the CPCB and State Boards. The Water Cess Act 1977 taxes water use. Jan Vishwas amendments (2023–24) replaced many jail terms with penalties. The Ganga Action Plan began in 1985. Namami Gange (2014) is run by the National Mission for Clean Ganga with sewage treatment as its core. The Ganga became a National River in 2008. Jal Jeevan Mission (2019) aims at tap water in every rural home. Under the 1974 Act, no one may discharge sewage or trade effluent into a stream without the State Board's consent. It was India's first modern pollution law. Under the Environment Protection Act 1986 the Centre sets effluent standards. Practical tools are sewage treatment plants (STPs), common effluent treatment plants (CETPs) and zero liquid discharge norms. Namami Gange also covers industrial effluent monitoring and riverfront development.
Quiet and slow

Causes: excess pesticide and fertiliser, industrial effluent, mining, solid waste, irrigation with polluted water. Result: salinity, alkalinity, loss of microbes, heavy metals entering food. The Soil Health Card scheme (2015) promotes balanced use. Organic farming schemes such as PKVY reduce chemical load. Contaminated site rules remain weak in India.
Rules and limits

Noise is measured in decibels (dB). The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 under the EPA give day (6 am to 10 pm) and night limits. Day/night limits in dB(A): industrial 75/70, commercial 65/55, residential 55/45, silence zone 50/40. Silence zones extend to 100 m around hospitals, schools and courts. Loudspeakers are restricted between 10 pm and 6 am with limited exceptions.
Thermal and marine

Thermal pollution comes from power plant coolant water. It lowers oxygen in rivers. Oil spills harm seabirds and coasts. The MARPOL convention (1973/78) regulates ship pollution. Plastic and microplastics now reach even the Himalaya and the deep sea. Thermal pollution also changes breeding and kills heat-sensitive fish because warm water holds less dissolved oxygen. Oil spills are cleaned with booms, skimmers and dispersants, and the Indian Coast Guard handles response under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan. Microplastics are particles under five millimetres and enter food chains through fish and salt.
Law is strong, enforcement is weak

State Pollution Control Boards are short of staff and funds, and sometimes politically pressured. Decriminalisation (Jan Vishwas) is defended as ease of doing business but criticised as weakening deterrence. The polluter pays principle is accepted, yet recovery of environmental compensation is slow. River cleaning has focused on building plants; poor running and no ecological flow remain problems. NGT orders and court-imposed environmental compensation have forced some cleanups, yet many orders go unmet. Audits have pointed to unspent funds and delays in river projects. Experts propose independent monitoring, real-time online emission monitoring, a larger role for communities, and treating wastewater as a resource for reuse in industry and farming.
Rivers and cases

The Yamuna in Delhi, the Ganga near Kanpur and the Adyar and Cooum in Chennai are standard examples. The NGT has monitored Ganga and Yamuna cleaning. The Supreme Court’s M.C. Mehta v Union of India (Ganga tanneries) and the Vellore Citizens case (1996) established the precautionary principle and polluter pays.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Despite crores spent, Indian rivers remain polluted. Why? Suggest reforms.” Structure: causes (sewage gap, industry, agriculture); programmes (GAP, Namami Gange); failures (design, running costs, ecological flow, governance); way forward (decentralised treatment, reuse, river basin authorities). Prelims tip: BOD high means worse water. Fluoride limit 1.5 mg/L. Silence zone 100 m. Water Act 1974.
Solid, Plastic, E-waste and Hazardous Waste
Waste is a governance test

India generates tens of millions of tonnes of solid waste a year, and city dumps like Ghazipur in Delhi are visible failures. UPSC asks about the rule sets, the EPR idea and global treaties. Learn each rule with its year. Mains likes the idea that waste is a resource problem, not just a disposal problem.
The waste hierarchy

Reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose. Landfill is the last option. A circular economy keeps materials in use. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) makes the maker of a product responsible for its waste after use. It is the main tool in Indian rules for plastics, e-waste, batteries and tyres.
Solid Waste Management Rules 2016

The 2016 rules replaced the 2000 rules. They require source segregation into wet, dry and domestic hazardous waste, extend to areas beyond municipal limits, bring in bulk waste generators , and push composting and waste-to-energy. The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 , notified in January 2026 and in force from 1 April 2026, replaced the 2016 rules. They require segregation into four streams: wet, dry, sanitary and special care waste. Related: Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0 aims at garbage-free cities. Indore is the model city.
Rules and bans

The Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 were amended in 2021. Identified single-use plastics were banned from 1 July 2022. Carry bag thickness was raised to 75 microns (September 2021) and 120 microns (December 2022). The 2022 EPR guidelines for plastic packaging set recycling targets and mandate registration on a central portal. Plastic credits can be traded.
E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022

India is among the largest producers of e-waste. The 2022 rules (in force April 2023) replaced the 2016 rules. They set EPR targets and certificates for producers, and cover refurbishers and recyclers. Informal recyclers handle most e-waste, exposing workers to lead, mercury and burning fumes. Linking them to formal channels is a major Mains point.
The family of rules

Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016 : includes control of cross-border movement. Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016 with colour-coded bags. Construction and Demolition Waste Rules 2016 . Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 with EPR. Basel Convention (1989) bans dumping of hazardous waste in poorer countries; Rotterdam (1998) is prior informed consent; Stockholm (2001) targets persistent organic pollutants.
The treaty talks

The UN agreed in 2022 to negotiate a legally binding plastics treaty. Talks in Busan (December 2024) and Geneva (August 2025) ended without agreement, split over production caps versus waste management. India’s stance favours waste management and common but differentiated responsibilities, and resists production caps.
EPR and the informal sector

EPR can fund recycling, but credits may be traded on paper without real collection. Critics say the rules ignore the role of waste pickers, who are the real recyclers. Waste-to-energy plants also face criticism for low-calorific mixed waste, air emissions and costs. Source segregation, not technology, is the weak link.
Cities and legacy dumps

Landfill fires and trash mountains at Ghazipur, Bhalswa and Deonar are recurring news. Programmes such as Swachh Bharat and bio-mining of legacy waste try to clear them. Indore, Surat and Ambikapur show that segregation and community systems work. Kerala’s Haritha Karma Sena uses women’s groups.
How to answer

Mains-style: “E-waste is an emerging threat. Examine India’s regulatory framework and gaps.” Structure: scale; rules (2016 then 2022 EPR); implementation gaps (informal sector, low collection); way forward (formalisation, design for repair, right to repair). Mains-style: “Discuss EPR as a tool for plastic waste management.” Prelims tip: Learn each year: SWM 2016, Plastic 2016 (amended 2021), E-waste 2022, Battery 2022. Basel = hazardous waste.
National Clean Air Programme, GRAP and Vehicle Norms
Air quality in the news

Delhi's winter smog makes air policy a yearly headline. Prelims asks about the NCAP, AQI categories, Bharat Stage norms and GRAP. Mains asks why the problem persists and which fixes work. Learn the figures and the institutions: CPCB, CAQM and state boards. Expect a table-style question linking AQI band, health effect and the GRAP stage that follows.
National Air Quality Index

The National AQI was launched in 2014 by the Government of India. It has six categories: Good (0-50), Satisfactory (51-100), Moderate (101-200), Poor (201-300), Very Poor (301-400) and Severe (401-500). It measures eight pollutants : PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3 and Pb. The CPCB runs the National Air Monitoring Programme. SAFAR (System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting) is run by IITM Pune and the IMD for big cities.
The 2019 programme

The National Clean Air Programme was launched in January 2019 . It is a time-bound, national-level plan. Original target: cut PM2.5 and PM10 by 20 to 30 percent by 2024 against 2017 levels. It was later raised to a 40 percent cut by 2025-26. It covers 131 non-attainment cities that failed the national standard for five years. The PRANA portal tracks progress. Funds go through the 15th Finance Commission grants for million-plus cities. It is not legally binding.
Bharat Stage norms

Bharat Stage (BS) norms are emission standards for engines, copied from the European model. BS-I started in 2000. India skipped BS-V and moved from BS-IV to BS-VI on 1 April 2020 , a leap that cut sulphur in fuel to 10 ppm. The next steps include the shift to E20 petrol, CNG buses in Delhi (after the Supreme Court order of 1998 in M.C. Mehta) and a push to electric vehicles . Vehicle scrappage policy (2021) removes old, polluting cars.
Graded Response Action Plan

GRAP is an emergency plan for Delhi-NCR, first notified in 2017 on the Supreme Court's direction. Actions escalate with air quality: Stage I (Poor): dust control, bans on burning waste. Stage II (Very Poor): more parking fees, fewer diesel generators. Stage III (Severe): halts on some construction, limits on BS-III petrol and BS-IV diesel vehicles. Stage IV (Severe plus): truck entry ban, schools may go online. The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) is the NCR body under the 2021 Act and runs GRAP.
Where the smog comes from

Main sources in Delhi: vehicles, road dust, industry, power plants, construction and, in October-November, stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana. Winter inversion traps the pollutants close to the ground. Other sources: burning of waste, biomass cooking and diesel generators. Ambient limits: the 2021 WHO guideline is 5 µg/m3 for annual PM2.5. The Indian standard is 40 µg/m3. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981 is the base law.
Why does it keep failing?

NCAP is not legally binding. Funds are often spent on road sweepers and not on source control. Many cities have too few monitors. The Delhi odd-even rule is cited as a short-term fix with small effect. Stubble burning needs farmer incentives for the Happy Seeder, biomass uses and crop shifts. Some argue the focus should shift to regional airsheds rather than city boundaries.
Health and cost

Air pollution is a leading risk factor for early death in India. Studies in the Lancet put deaths in the lakhs per year. Smaller cities like Byrnihat (Meghalaya) and Ghaziabad often top the list. The Ujjwala Yojana (2016) cuts indoor smoke, and PM Surya Ghar and EVs target outdoor sources.
Quick table

AQI: 2014; six bands; eight pollutants. NCAP: 2019; 131 cities; 20-30 percent, later 40 percent. BS-VI: 1 April 2020. GRAP: four stages; run by CAQM. CAQM: statutory body since 2021. Note also that PM2.5 are particles under 2.5 micrometres, which reach deep into the lungs and blood.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "AQI includes which pollutants?" "BS-VI norms came into force in which year?" (2020). Mains-style: "Why is air pollution in Delhi-NCR a recurring crisis? Evaluate NCAP." Structure: sources; health costs; NCAP and GRAP; gaps (non-binding, funds); way forward (airshed approach, public transport, stubble alternatives). Use a number: the WHO annual PM2.5 limit of 5 against India's 40 shows how big the gap is.
Water Pollution Laws and Namami Gange
Rivers in the exam

The Ganga is a standing GS3 theme. Prelims asks for dates (Ganga Action Plan, NMCG, Namami Gange) and bodies. Mains asks why clean-up has taken decades and what a better design looks like. The water law story is also a story of institutions: boards, missions and courts.
Water Act 1974 and others

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was the first environmental law of its kind. It was passed under Article 252 , when states asked Parliament to legislate. It set up the CPCB (1974) and State Pollution Control Boards , and requires consent to establish and operate for industries. The Water Cess Act, 1977 taxes water use by industry to fund the boards. The Environment (Protection) Act 1986 adds penalties and standards. Pollution is measured by BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) and DO (dissolved oxygen).
From GAP to Namami Gange

Ganga Action Plan (1985): launched by Rajiv Gandhi at Varanasi; focus on sewage treatment. National River Conservation Plan (1995): expanded to other rivers. National Ganga River Basin Authority (2009): chaired by the PM; the Ganga was declared the National River in 2008. Namami Gange (2014-15): an integrated mission with a budget of about Rs 20,000 crore for 2015-20, since extended. The National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG) is the implementing body and became an authority under the EPA in 2016.
Pillars of the mission

The mission has several pillars: sewage treatment infrastructure , river-front development (ghats), river surface cleaning , afforestation , industrial effluent monitoring , biodiversity (dolphins, turtles) and public participation . The Hybrid Annuity Model and One City One Operator were used to make plants work for years. Arth Ganga links the river to the local economy. It focuses on natural farming along banks, tourism and water use.
Legal personhood and cases

In M.C. Mehta v Union of India (1988) the Supreme Court ordered tanneries at Kanpur to treat effluent. In March 2017 , the Uttarakhand High Court declared the Ganga and Yamuna to have the status of legal persons. The Supreme Court stayed the order. The NGT has also ordered no dumping on Ganga banks. The polluter pays principle and precautionary principle were laid down in cases such as *Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action* (1996) and *Vellore Citizens* (1996).
Beyond Ganga

The Yamuna Action Plan (since 1993) has taken large sums but the river remains highly polluted in Delhi, where most pollution comes from drains. The Jal Shakti Ministry (2019) merged water departments. Jal Jeevan Mission (2019) brings tap water to rural homes, and Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019) manages groundwater with communities. Among the issues: untreated sewage, industrial effluent, agricultural runoff, sand mining and dams that reduce flow.
Treatment or flow?

Experts argue that e-flow (environmental flow) matters as much as sewage plants. A river with water and silt cleans itself, but dams and diversions cut flow. Another issue is that spending on plants did not match running costs. The hybrid model, cleaner industry and decentralised treatment are practical fixes. Critics say progress on the ground is slow.
Numbers and sites

The Ganga basin has about 40 percent of India's people. Kanpur tanneries, Varanasi ghats and Haridwar-Rishikesh are focus points. The CPCB monitors water quality at many stations and flags polluted river stretches. Kumbh crowds create short pulses of waste. The Gangetic dolphin and the Hilsa fish are indicators of recovery.
Dates in a line

Water Act: 1974; CPCB: 1974. Ganga Action Plan: 1985. Ganga National River: 2008. NGRBA: 2009; NMCG registered as a society 2011. Namami Gange: 2014-15. Legal person status: Uttarakhand HC, 2017 (stayed). Also remember: Water Cess Act 1977; Jal Shakti Ministry 2019; Jal Jeevan Mission 2019; Atal Bhujal Yojana 2019.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which Act created the Central Pollution Control Board?" (Water Act 1974). "The Ganga Action Plan began in" (1985). Mains-style: "Despite large expenditure, why is the Ganga still polluted? Suggest a way forward." Structure: plans and spending; reasons (sewage gap, industry, low flow, weak enforcement); Namami Gange reforms; e-flow and community role.
Marine Pollution, Oil Spills and Ocean Acidification
Seas as sink

Oceans absorb heat, carbon and waste. Prelims asks about spills, conventions (MARPOL, London), acidification and dead zones. Mains asks about the Indian coast and the Blue Economy. It also links to coral reefs, fisheries and climate. Expect a one-line match: spill name with place, or convention with subject.
Land and sea

About 80 percent of marine pollution comes from land: sewage, plastics, fertiliser run-off, industrial waste. The rest comes from ships (oil, garbage, ballast water) and accidents. Plastic is now found from the surface to the deep sea, and microplastics enter food chains. Ocean gyres collect floating debris. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch lies between Hawaii and California.
Cases to know

Exxon Valdez (1989): Alaska; one of the best-known tanker spills. Deepwater Horizon (2010): Gulf of Mexico; the largest marine oil spill in history by volume. MV Wakashio (2020): Mauritius, ran aground on a coral reef. Ennore, Chennai (January 2017): two ships collided and oil reached the beach. X-Press Pearl (2021): Sri Lanka; plastic pellets and chemicals. Oil coats birds and fur, blocks light and harms fish eggs.
Response methods

Spill response uses booms (floating barriers), skimmers , dispersants and in-situ burning . Bioremediation uses oil-eating bacteria. The Indian Coast Guard is the national response agency under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan (1996). Dispersants break oil into droplets but can also be toxic. Prevention is better: double-hulled tankers, safe routes and strict inspection.
International law

MARPOL 73/78 (IMO): prevents pollution from ships. Six Annexes: oil, noxious liquids, harmful packaged goods, sewage, garbage, air pollution. London Convention (1972) and its Protocol: dumping of wastes at sea. UNCLOS (1982): the law of the sea; EEZ of 200 nautical miles. Ballast Water Convention (2004) controls invasive species carried by ships. OPRC 1990: preparedness against oil pollution. India is a party to MARPOL and UNCLOS.
The other CO2 problem

The ocean absorbs about a quarter of human CO2. The gas reacts with water to form carbonic acid and lowers pH . Since the industrial era surface pH has fallen by about 0.1 units (from about 8.2 to 8.1), around 30 percent more acidic. Acidification makes it harder for corals, shellfish and pteropods to build calcium carbonate shells. It joins warming and deoxygenation as threats. Coral bleaching is caused by warmth, not acid, but reefs face both.
Hypoxia

Fertiliser run-off feeds algae. When they die, bacteria use oxygen, and dead zones form. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone, fed by the Mississippi River, is a famous example. Red tides (harmful algal blooms) are another sign. India: the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal have low-oxygen layers, and blooms have affected Kerala and Odisha coasts.
Coast and policy

India has about 11,098 km of coastline including islands (the 2023 figure; earlier 7,516 km). The Coastal Regulation Zone rules limit building near the coast. Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar (2022) was a coastal cleanup drive. India's Blue Economy policy and the Deep Ocean Mission (2021) raise both use and risk. The National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR) works on coastal health.
Key points

80 percent of marine pollution comes from land. MARPOL 73/78: ship pollution. London Convention: dumping at sea. Ocean acidification: pH down by about 0.1. ICG: lead for oil spills. Also hold the numbers: 80 percent from land, pH down by 0.1, EEZ 200 nautical miles, ICG plan 1996.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which convention deals with pollution from ships?" (MARPOL). "Ocean acidification affects which organisms?" (corals, molluscs). Mains-style: "Discuss the causes and consequences of marine pollution. What steps can India take?" Structure: land and sea sources; spills; acidification; legal framework; Indian measures; way forward. Close with one Indian step, such as the Deep Ocean Mission or Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar.
Plastic, Solid Waste and E-waste Rules and EPR
Rules are asked by name

Waste rules change often, and UPSC tests the latest ones. Prelims asks about EPR, the 2022 single-use plastic ban and the 3R principle. Mains asks why rules fail on the ground. Know each rule's year and its central idea. Also know the one-line meaning of each rule, since options often swap years between waste streams.
The 2016 framework

Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2018, 2021, 2022) introduced Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for producers, importers and brand owners. They apply to the whole country, not only to cities. Local bodies manage collection and segregation. The 2021 amendment banned identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022 : plastic sticks for ice cream, earbuds, balloons, cutlery, plates and straws. It also raised the minimum thickness of plastic carry bags to 75 microns from 30 September 2021 and 120 microns from 31 December 2022.
Who pays

EPR means producers are responsible for the waste of their product after use. They must collect or fund collection and recycling. The EPR Guidelines of February 2022 set categories of plastic packaging, targets for recycling and use of recycled content, and an online portal with certificates traded between firms. The idea comes from the polluter pays principle . The Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 and E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 also use EPR.
SWM Rules 2016

The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 replaced the Municipal Solid Wastes Rules of 2000. They apply beyond municipal areas and cover urban agglomerations and census towns. Waste must be segregated at source into wet, dry and domestic hazardous. They push composting, bio-methanation and waste-to-energy and ask for waste-picker integration. The Swachh Bharat Mission (2014; Urban 2.0 in 2021) supports it. Landfill legacy sites like Ghazipur, Bhalswa and Okhla in Delhi are a burden.
E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022

India is among the largest e-waste producers. The 2022 Rules (effective 1 April 2023 ) cover more electronic items, set EPR targets and certificates for producers, and bring in registration of recyclers . They add a refurbisher category and make recyclers register, so that informal and unsafe recycling is pushed out. Other waste streams: Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016, Construction and Demolition Waste Rules 2016, and the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules 2016 .
The waste hierarchy

The hierarchy is Reduce, Reuse, Recycle , with Refuse and Recover sometimes added. Recycling is the lowest rung in preference after reduction. Circular economy ideas aim to keep materials in use. Biodegradable and compostable plastics need separate standards, and "oxo-degradable" claims are not trusted. India generates around 3.5 million tonnes of plastic waste each year (CPCB estimates for 2019-20).
Ban or manage?

A ban on single-use items is easy to announce but hard to enforce, since substitutes may not be cheaper or better. Informal waste pickers do most recycling and need a place in the system. EPR can shift costs to consumers and is hard to audit. A balanced view: combine bans on low-value items, EPR for the rest, better collection and consumer awareness.
Waste and cities

Indore is the model for clean city ranking. Sikkim banned plastic bottles early, and several states had bag bans before the national rule. The National Green Tribunal has pushed states on landfills and plastic. India raised the issue at the UN Environment Assembly in 2022, where member states agreed to work towards a global plastics treaty (INC process, 2022 onward).
Rules at a glance

PWM Rules 2016; ban on listed single-use plastic 1 July 2022. SWM Rules 2016. E-Waste Rules 2022, effective April 2023. BWM Rules 2022 for batteries. EPR: producer responsibility; online portal. Remember that Bio-Medical, C&D and Hazardous Waste Rules are all of 2016, with the plastic and SWM Rules.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Extended Producer Responsibility is based on which principle?" (polluter pays). "Which year saw the ban on identified single-use plastics?" (2022). Mains-style: "Is a ban on single-use plastics enough? Suggest a comprehensive approach." Structure: scale; rules; EPR; informal sector; alternatives; consumer role; global treaty. Add the informal sector and a number on India's plastic waste to lift the answer.
Eutrophication, Heavy Metals and Bioremediation
Frequent technical terms

Prelims uses these terms in tricky statements: BOD, eutrophication, heavy metals, bioremediation and phytoremediation. Each is simple once you see how it works. Mains links them to rivers, farming and industrial disasters. Expect a statement-type question on BOD and DO, so learn which one rises and which one falls with pollution.
Too many nutrients

Eutrophication is over-enrichment of water with nutrients, mainly nitrogen and phosphorus from fertiliser, sewage and detergents. It makes algae bloom. When they die, bacteria use up oxygen ( BOD rises, DO falls) and fish die. Lakes may turn into marsh over time. Natural eutrophication takes centuries. Cultural eutrophication caused by people is rapid. A bloom can also release toxins. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone and Indian lakes like Dal, Hussain Sagar and Ooty are examples.
BOD, COD and DO

DO: dissolved oxygen. Healthy water holds above 5 mg per litre. BOD: the oxygen needed by microbes to break down organic matter. High BOD means heavy organic pollution. COD: chemical oxygen demand, a measure of all chemically oxidisable matter. Indicator organisms like coliform bacteria show sewage contamination. Clean river targets set BOD below 3 mg per litre for bathing water (CPCB class A and B criteria).
Poisons that stay

Heavy metals such as mercury, lead, cadmium, arsenic and chromium do not break down. They bioaccumulate and biomagnify. Mercury: Minamata disease (Japan, 1956). Cadmium: Itai-itai disease (Japan). Lead: harms children's brains; leaded petrol was phased out in India by 2000. Arsenic: groundwater in West Bengal, Bihar, Assam and the Gangetic plain. Fluoride: causes fluorosis in Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh. The Bhopal gas tragedy (1984, methyl isocyanate leak) is the key industrial disaster.
Using living things to clean

Bioremediation uses microbes or plants to break down or remove pollutants. In-situ: done at the site. Ex-situ: soil or water is taken elsewhere. Bioaugmentation: adding specially grown microbes. Biostimulation: adding nutrients to help local microbes. Phytoremediation: plants take up metals, such as sunflower and Indian mustard. Mycoremediation: fungi. Oil-eating bacteria are used in oil spills. Wetlands and constructed reed beds clean waste water cheaply. Bioremediation is slower but cheaper than digging up soil.
Other terms often mixed in

Biomagnification: rise in concentration up the food chain. Bioaccumulation: build-up in one organism. Algal bloom: rapid algae growth. Thermal pollution: warm water from power plants lowers oxygen. Radioactive fallout: Chernobyl (1986), Fukushima (2011). India's standards for effluents come under the Environment (Protection) Rules 1986. Zero Liquid Discharge is required of many industries on the Ganga.
Cure or prevention?

Bioremediation sounds clean, but it works only for certain pollutants and conditions. Heavy metals can only be moved or locked, not destroyed. Many experts say that preventing pollution at the source, through effluent treatment and less fertiliser, is far cheaper than cleaning later. Farmers rely on subsidised urea, so nitrogen runs high. Fertiliser reform and neem-coated urea (2015) are part of the answer.
Case examples

The Yamuna has very high BOD and froth below Delhi from detergents and sewage. Kolleru and Vembanad show nutrient pollution. Punjab's Malwa belt has cancers linked in public debate to heavy metals and pesticides in water, still a contested subject. Arsenic in the Ganga delta region affects millions. Phytoremediation trials use water hyacinth for metals.
Definitions

Eutrophication: nutrient overload, low oxygen. BOD: oxygen microbes need to break down organic matter. Heavy metals: persist and biomagnify. Bioremediation: living organisms clean pollutants. Phytoremediation: plants do it. Also remember: heavy metals do not break down, and bioremediation uses living organisms. Phytoremediation uses plants; mycoremediation uses fungi.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "A high BOD indicates" (heavy organic pollution). "Which of these is used in phytoremediation?" "Eutrophication is caused by excess of" (nitrogen and phosphorus). Mains-style: "Explain eutrophication and its effects on Indian water bodies. How can it be controlled?" Structure: definition; causes; chain of events; effects; Indian examples; control (sewage treatment, fertiliser use, wetlands, bioremediation).
Deforestation, Desertification and Land Degradation
Land is a climate and livelihood issue

Nearly 30 percent of India’s land is degraded. UPSC links this to food security, floods, migration and climate. The key laws and conventions (UNCCD, Forest Conservation Act, FRA) appear in Prelims and Mains. The core idea is Land Degradation Neutrality : no net loss of healthy land.
Three linked terms

Deforestation is clearing forest for other uses. Land degradation is loss of productivity from erosion, salinity, waterlogging or loss of vegetation. Desertification is degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas from climate and human activity. It does not mean desert spreading by sand alone. Water erosion is the largest cause of degradation in India, followed by vegetation loss and wind erosion.
Why it happens

Agriculture expansion, shifting cultivation (jhum) with short fallows. Mining, dams and roads; urban sprawl. Overgrazing and fuelwood collection. Unsustainable irrigation causing salinity and waterlogging, for example in Punjab and Haryana. Climate change: drought and extreme rain.
India’s land

The SAC-ISRO Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas reported that about 97.85 million hectares (nearly 29.7 percent of India’s area) was degraded in 2018–19. The main hotspots are Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat and Delhi. India has pledged to restore 26 million hectares by 2030 under the Bonn Challenge and the UNCCD, and to create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent. The atlas shows water erosion as the largest single process of degradation, followed by vegetation degradation and wind erosion. Desertification is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas; the Thar is the main arid region, and the Aravalli range has also lost cover. Degradation lowers soil carbon, water-holding capacity and crop yield.
The global treaty

The UN Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted in 1994 (Paris) and entered into force in 1996. It is a result of the 1992 Rio Summit and is the only legally binding convention on land. It has a bottom-up approach with national action programmes. India hosted UNCCD COP14 in Greater Noida in 2019. The Delhi Declaration stressed land restoration and gender. Other efforts: the Bonn Challenge (2011), Africa’s Great Green Wall , and India’s plan for an Aravalli green belt.
Forest Conservation Act and the 2023 change

The Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 bars diversion of forest land without Central approval. In 1996 the T.N. Godavarman case widened the meaning of forest to its dictionary sense. The 2023 amendment (renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam) limits the Act to land notified as forest or recorded as forest after 25 October 1980. It exempts some linear projects near borders and security infrastructure up to set sizes. The Supreme Court has directed that the wider 1996 definition be applied for now (as of 2024).
Rights and money

The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights for Scheduled Tribes and other traditional dwellers. CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act 2016) pays for afforestation when forest land is diverted. Joint Forest Management (1990) involves village committees. Green India Mission is under the NAPCC. The campaign “Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam” (2024) encourages tree planting.
Compensatory afforestation is not equal

Critics say planting trees elsewhere does not replace a natural forest. Plantations store less biodiversity and are often on poor land. Funds sit unspent for years. Development needs, such as the Great Nicobar project and coal mining in Hasdeo Arand, create a standing conflict between growth and forest.
Examples

Ravines of the Chambal, salinity in the Indo-Gangetic canal belt, and loss of mangroves in the Sundarbans are land degradation cases. Rajasthan’s Thar is spreading at the edges. Sikkim and Mizoram show better forest outcomes with community control. Meghalaya and Nagaland have community forests. The Chambal ravines were formed by gully erosion of soft alluvium. Canal irrigation without drainage causes waterlogging and salinity in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh. In the Sundarbans, rising seas, cyclones and shrimp farming damage mangroves. Community forest management, such as Joint Forest Management and Van Panchayats in Uttarakhand, shows that local control can improve forest condition.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What is land degradation? How does it affect food security, and what steps has India taken?” Structure: definition; extent (nearly 30 percent); causes; effects on yield and livelihoods; policy (soil health card, watershed development, Bonn commitment, UNCCD); way forward. Mains-style: “Critically evaluate the 2023 Forest Conservation amendment.” Prelims tip: UNCCD 1994, entered into force 1996, COP14 in India 2019. Bonn Challenge 2011. Prelims tip: the World Day to Combat Desertification is 17 June. The Forest Survey of India publishes the India State of Forest Report every two years. In answers use data from the atlas and name schemes: Soil Health Card (2015), watershed development under PMKSY, the Green India Mission and CAMPA funds. End with land degradation neutrality, which is SDG target 15.3.
Wetlands, Mangroves and Coral Reefs
Coastal and wetland ecosystems are Prelims gold

Ramsar sites, Montreux Record, mangroves and coral bleaching appear in nearly every Prelims. Mains asks about coastal regulation and blue carbon. These ecosystems protect coasts, store carbon and feed millions. They are also among the most threatened. These ecosystems sit at the boundary of land and water. Wetlands hold flood water, mangroves slow storm surge, and coral reefs break waves. They also store large amounts of carbon, called blue carbon, in plants and mud. Link each ecosystem to its law or scheme and a named site; examples such as Chilika, Sundarbans and Lakshadweep appear often.
Definition and Ramsar

The Ramsar Convention (Iran, 1971; in force 1975) is the global treaty for wetlands. It promotes wise use . Sites are listed under the Ramsar List. The Montreux Record lists sites with damaged ecology. In India it includes Keoladeo and Loktak. World Wetlands Day is 2 February. India’s Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017 replaced the 2010 rules and set a State Wetland Authority. Ramsar defines wetlands broadly: marshes, fens, peatlands, lakes, rivers, mangroves, coral reefs, and even paddy fields, plus marine water up to six metres deep at low tide. Wetlands filter water, recharge groundwater, store floodwater and support birds and fish. The Convention rests on three pillars: wise use, listing of sites, and international cooperation.
As of 2026

India’s first Ramsar sites were Chilika and Keoladeo (1981). As of 2026, India has about 100 Ramsar sites (reports during the year range from 98 to 103), the most in Asia. India ranks first in Asia and third in the world by number. Tamil Nadu has the most sites. The Sundarbans is the largest Ramsar site in India by area.
Salt-loving forests

Mangroves grow in the intertidal zone. Adaptations: pneumatophores (breathing roots), stilt roots , viviparity (seeds germinate on the tree) and salt excretion. They guard against cyclones and tsunamis, nurse fish and store “blue carbon.” India has roughly 5,000 sq km of mangroves (ISFR). West Bengal (Sundarbans) has the biggest share, followed by Gujarat and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Policy

Budget 2023–24 announced MISHTI (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes) and Amrit Dharohar for wetlands. Mangroves are protected in CRZ-I under the Coastal Regulation Zone rules. The Green Credit Programme also lists mangrove restoration as an activity. MISHTI aims to restore mangroves along the coast and the salt pans, using convergence with MGNREGS and CAMPA funds. Amrit Dharohar encourages the wise use of wetlands and aims to boost bird tourism and local incomes. Under CRZ rules, the zones range from CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive) to CRZ-IV (waters), and the 2019 notification set no-development zones near the shore.
Living limestone

Corals are animals (polyps) with algae called zooxanthellae living inside them. They give colour and food. Reefs are fringing , barrier or atoll . They need warm (about 23 to 29 °C), clear, shallow, saline water. They cover under 1 percent of the ocean but support about a quarter of marine species. Corals build a calcium carbonate skeleton, and reefs form over thousands of years. In India reefs are found in the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Reef algae need light, so reefs stay in shallow water and avoid muddy river mouths. Reefs protect coasts from waves and support fisheries and tourism.
Threat

When water is too warm, corals expel algae and turn white: bleaching . Other threats: ocean acidification, pollution, dynamite fishing and cyclones. The world has seen a fourth global bleaching event since 2023, the most widespread on record. India’s reef regions are the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
CRZ Notification 2019

The Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019 replaced the 2011 rules. CRZ-I is ecologically sensitive (mangroves, corals; with an inter-tidal part), CRZ-II is built-up urban shore, CRZ-III is rural and undeveloped, and CRZ-IV covers water area up to 12 nautical miles. Critics argue the 2019 rules allowed more building near beaches. Supporters say they help livelihoods and give clearer zones.
Examples

Chilika (Odisha), Loktak (Manipur), Sundarbans , Bhitarkanika mangroves and Gulf of Mannar corals are key cases. Kolkata’s East Kolkata Wetlands treat the city’s sewage naturally. Wetlands are lost to reclamation and encroachment in Bengaluru, Chennai and Srinagar, and floods in Chennai (2015) showed the cost.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Why are wetlands called the kidneys of the landscape? What threats do Indian wetlands face?” Structure: functions; Ramsar and rules; threats (encroachment, sewage, invasives); remedies (wise use, community role, Amrit Dharohar). Prelims tip: Montreux Record: Keoladeo and Loktak. First Ramsar sites: Chilika and Keoladeo. Mangroves are CRZ-I. Know the five reef areas.
Ramsar Convention and India's Ramsar Sites
A near-certain Prelims topic

Ramsar questions appear almost every year: which site is in which state, which sites are on the Montreux Record, what the criteria are, and how many sites India has. Site counts keep rising, so exams also test the latest additions. This lesson holds the stable facts first and the changing numbers clearly marked "as of".
What the Convention is

The Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat was signed at Ramsar, Iran , on 2 February 1971 and came into force in 1975 . World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February . The Secretariat is at Gland, Switzerland . India became a party on 1 February 1982 . It is the oldest modern global environmental treaty on one ecosystem. Its three pillars are wise use of all wetlands, designating Ramsar sites, and international cooperation . A listing does not take land from national control, and the site stays under national law.
Nine criteria for listing

A wetland qualifies if it meets at least one of nine criteria . Criterion 1: a representative, rare or unique wetland type. Criteria 2 to 6: biodiversity of species and communities. Criterion 5 is 20,000 or more waterbirds . Criterion 6 is 1 percent of a waterbird population. Criteria 7 and 8: fish. Criterion 9: 1 percent of a non-bird wetland-dependent animal population. The definition of wetland is broad. It includes marshes, lakes, rivers, peatlands, mangroves, coral reefs, paddy fields, and marine water up to six metres deep at low tide.
Sites under threat

The Montreux Record is a list of Ramsar sites where changes in ecological character have happened, are happening or are likely. It was set up in 1990 at a conference in Montreux, Switzerland. A listing is meant to draw help, not to punish. India has two sites on the record : Keoladeo National Park (Rajasthan) and Loktak Lake (Manipur). Chilika (Odisha) was put on it and then removed in 2002 , after restoration work and opening a new mouth to the sea. It was the first Asian site removed, and later won a Ramsar award.
How the number grew (as of dates)

India's first two sites, Chilika and Keoladeo , were listed in 1981-82. The count was about 26 in 2014 . It rose sharply in recent years: about 49 as of August 2022 about 75 as of February 2023 about 85 as of August 2024 about 89 to 91 as of 2025 Counts change, so check the latest list. India has the largest Ramsar network in South Asia . Tamil Nadu has the most sites of any state, and Uttar Pradesh is next. The Sundarbans (West Bengal, 2019) is the largest Indian Ramsar site by area.
Names to learn

Rajasthan: Keoladeo (Bharatpur), Sambhar Lake (salt lake). Odisha: Chilika (largest coastal lagoon, brackish), Bhitarkanika mangroves. Manipur: Loktak (floating phumdis, Keibul Lamjao, sangai deer). Punjab: Harike, Kanjli, Ropar. Kerala: Ashtamudi, Vembanad-Kol, Sasthamkotta. Andhra Pradesh: Kolleru. Gujarat: Nalsarovar. Ladakh: Tso Moriri. J&K: Wular, Hokersar. Assam: Deepor Beel. Maharashtra: Lonar Lake (2020), Nandur Madhameshwar. Madhya Pradesh: Bhoj Wetland, Sakhya Sagar.
Rules and schemes

India has no wetland-specific Act. The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 replaced the 2010 rules under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 . They give State Wetlands Authorities the task of listing and regulating wetlands and set up a National Wetlands Committee . They ban conversion for non-wetland use, solid waste dumping and industry in notified wetlands. They exclude river channels, paddy fields and areas under the CRZ rules. Schemes: the National Wetland Conservation Programme (1985-86), later merged into the National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA, 2013) . Amrit Dharohar (announced in the Union Budget 2023-24 and launched in June 2023) aims at the wise use of wetlands, local livelihoods, ecotourism and carbon stock.
Listing versus protection

A Ramsar tag brings attention and tourists, but it does not give legal protection by itself. Many sites sit inside national parks, like Keoladeo, and are protected by other laws. Others, like urban lakes and river stretches, have weak management. Critics say states race to add sites for numbers. Supporters say listing brings management plans, funds and community involvement.
Threats and examples

Keoladeo suffers from lack of water from the Gambhir river and invasive grass. Loktak's water level is changed by the Ithai barrage, which flooded phumdis and hurt fish. Harike is hit by water hyacinth and pollution. Wular and Dal face silt and encroachment. Wetlands also store flood water, recharge aquifers and hold carbon. India's wetlands cover about 4.6 percent of land (Space Applications Centre atlas, 2011).
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which Indian sites are on the Montreux Record?" (Keoladeo, Loktak). "Ramsar sites are designated under which criteria?" (nine). "Which is the largest brackish water lagoon in India?" (Chilika). Mains-style: "Why are wetlands called kidneys of the landscape? Discuss India's steps for their conservation." Structure: functions; Ramsar and numbers (as of year); Wetland Rules 2017; Amrit Dharohar; threats; community role; way forward.
Coastal Regulation Zone, Mangroves and Blue Carbon
Coast, climate and development

The coast faces cyclones, sea-level rise and building pressure. Prelims asks about CRZ categories, mangrove species and sites, and blue carbon. Mains asks if CRZ relaxations help or harm. Mangroves also feature in climate questions as cheap protection. Expect a question that pairs a CRZ category with its description.
The legal base

The Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification was first issued in 1991 under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. It was revised in 2011 and replaced by the CRZ Notification 2019 . CRZ covers the land up to 500 metres from the High Tide Line (HTL) on the sea side, the land along tidal-influenced water bodies, and the waters up to 12 nautical miles seaward. The National Coastal Zone Management Authority and State authorities enforce it. A separate Island Protection Zone notification (2011) covers Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep.
What each zone means

CRZ-I: ecologically sensitive areas (mangroves, corals, turtle nesting grounds, salt marshes) and the intertidal zone. Little or no building. CRZ-II: urban shoreline already built up. Construction allowed on the landward side of the existing road. CRZ-III: rural and undeveloped coast. A no-development zone of 200 m from the HTL; densely populated rural areas (CRZ-IIIA) have 50 m after 2019. CRZ-IV: water area from low tide line to 12 nautical miles, plus tidal water bodies. Fishing allowed, no solid waste dumping. The 2019 rules allow some tourism facilities and use floor space index relaxation in urban areas.
Salt-loving forests

Mangroves grow in tidal mud in the tropics. They have pneumatophores (breathing roots), prop roots and vivipary (seeds sprout on the tree). Species: Rhizophora , Avicennia , and Heritiera fomes (Sundari, which gave the Sundarbans its name). India has about 4,990 sq km of mangroves (ISFR 2021, roughly 0.15 percent of land). West Bengal has the largest share (Sundarbans), followed by Gujarat and Andaman and Nicobar. Bhitarkanika in Odisha has the saltwater crocodile and Olive Ridley nesting nearby. Mangroves cushion cyclones and tsunamis, trap sediment, and serve as fish nurseries.
Carbon in coastal systems

Blue carbon is carbon stored by coastal and marine ecosystems: mangroves, seagrass meadows and salt marshes . They store carbon in the soil for centuries, often more per hectare than land forests. Draining or clearing them releases it. The Blue Carbon Initiative is run by Conservation International, IUCN and UNESCO IOC. India started a MISHTI scheme (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes) in 2023 and has launched blue carbon projects in the Sundarbans and Odisha. Blue carbon is also a topic for carbon markets and NDCs.
What damages the coast

Aquaculture ponds (shrimp farms), ports, tourism, sand mining, and sea-level rise eat into mangroves. Coral and seagrass beds suffer from trawling and bleaching. Mumbai and Kerala lost large mangrove areas to land reclamation. The Supreme Court's S. Jagannath v Union of India (1996) is the standard case: it banned intensive shrimp farming inside the CRZ. The Bombay High Court (2018) ordered strong protection of mangroves.
Other coastal ecosystems

Coral reefs in India are at the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar, and the Gulf of Kutch. They are protected as Schedule I animals under the WPA, and corals need clear, warm, shallow water. Bleaching happens when stress makes corals expel their symbiotic algae ( zooxanthellae ). Seagrass meadows feed dugongs, which are Schedule I and live in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay and Andaman waters. The Gulf of Kutch and Gulf of Mannar marine national parks (both 1982) were among India's first.
Relaxation or protection?

CRZ 2019 gave the states more say and cut the no-development zone in some areas, which supporters say helps fishers and ports. Critics say it weakens defences against cyclones. The Swaminathan Committee (2005) and Shailesh Nayak Committee (2014) shaped these rules. A balanced answer: protect sensitive ecosystems fully, allow livelihoods for traditional fishers, and plan for sea-level rise.
Cyclones and communities

Odisha's cyclone losses fell after better warning and shelters, and mangrove belts add a green shield. After the 2004 tsunami, studies noted that villages behind mangroves in Tamil Nadu fared better. Fishing communities want rights over the shore, and the Kerala coast sees erosion from sea walls and ports.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "CRZ-III is" (rural, undeveloped, 200 m no-development zone). "Sundarbans is dominated by which mangrove tree?" (Sundari). Mains-style: "Discuss the role of mangroves in coastal protection and climate mitigation. Do CRZ rules protect them?" Structure: functions; blue carbon; CRZ categories; threats; relaxations; way forward (MISHTI, local participation).
Forest Cover in India and the ISFR
Numbers asked every year

Each new ISFR gives fresh numbers, and Prelims often asks about the state with the highest forest cover or the target in the National Forest Policy. Mains asks whether cover really means healthy forest. This lesson holds the definitions and the figures with their years.
The ISFR

The India State of Forest Report (ISFR) is published every two years by the Forest Survey of India (FSI) , Dehradun (set up in 1981). It uses satellite data (Resourcesat) and field checks. It reports forest cover (all land over one hectare with tree canopy density above 10 percent, whatever the owner) and tree cover (patches under one hectare, outside forest). Recorded forest area is a legal term for land recorded as forest in revenue records. It is different from cover.
What dense means

Very Dense Forest (VDF): canopy density 70 percent and above. Moderately Dense Forest (MDF): 40 to 70 percent. Open Forest (OF): 10 to 40 percent. Scrub: below 10 percent. The ISFR also reports mangrove cover, carbon stock in forests, bamboo area, and forest fire alerts. India reports its forest carbon sink to the UNFCCC, and a stated goal is an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2030.
Cover over time (check the latest)

ISFR 2021: forest cover about 7.13 lakh sq km , 21.71 percent of area; tree cover 2.91 percent; total about 24.62 percent. ISFR 2023: forest cover about 7.15 lakh sq km (21.76 percent) ; tree cover 3.41 percent; total about 25.17 percent . Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest area. Mizoram has the highest percentage of forest cover among states (above 84 percent in ISFR 2021). Among Union Territories, Lakshadweep is highest. States showing large gains in recent reports include Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Telangana, while losses are seen in the North-East.
Targets and plans

The National Forest Policy 1952 and 1988 set the goal of 33 percent of land under forest or tree cover, with 66 percent in hills. The 1988 policy puts conservation first and calls for people's involvement ( Joint Forest Management , 1990). The Green India Mission (under NAPCC) aims to increase and improve forest cover. The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 funds replanting. India's Bonn Challenge pledge is 26 million hectares of degraded land to be restored by 2030.
Champion and Seth

Champion and Seth (1968) classified Indian forests into 16 major types . Tropical moist deciduous and tropical dry deciduous forests cover the largest area. Tropical wet evergreen forests are found in the Western Ghats, the North-East and the Andaman. Sal and teak are major timber species. Mangroves and montane types complete the list. Plantations and monocultures can raise "cover" without raising biodiversity.
Gadgil and Kasturirangan

The Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel (Madhav Gadgil, 2011) suggested the whole range be an ecologically sensitive area with three zones. The High-Level Working Group (K. Kasturirangan, 2013) cut this to 37 percent of the area (about 59,940 sq km ) as ESA across six states. States opposed both, citing farmers and mining. MoEFCC has issued repeated draft notifications on the ESA since 2014. A final notification is still debated (as of recent years).
Is more cover better?

Critics say the ISFR counts plantations, orchards and even coconut groves as forest, so the rise masks the loss of natural forest. Open forests are growing but VDF area changes are small. Diversion of forest for mines and dams is a leading concern, and the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act 2023 added more debates on this.
People and fire

About 300 million people live near forests, and Non-Timber Forest Produce (NTFP) is a key livelihood for tribal families. Forest fire is a big risk in Uttarakhand and Odisha during summer. FSI sends fire alerts to forest staff using satellite data. Forest fire alerts, NTFP income and the 300 million forest-edge population are useful lines for a Mains answer.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Which state has the highest forest cover in percentage?" (Mizoram). "Which body publishes ISFR?" (FSI). "National Forest Policy 1988 target?" (33 percent). Mains-style: "Examine the trends in India's forest cover. Does an increase in cover mean better forests?" Structure: ISFR figures; types and density; plantations versus natural forests; policy tools; threats; way forward.
Desertification, UNCCD and Land Degradation Neutrality
Land is a climate and food issue

Soil loss and desert spread threaten farm output and rural jobs. Prelims asks about UNCCD, Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) and the India hosting of COP14. Mains asks about causes and solutions. This lesson focuses on the global treaty and India's numbers. A common trap is to treat desertification as the growth of existing deserts. It is a degradation process in dry lands.
Terms

Land degradation is the loss of land's productivity. Desertification is degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas caused by climate and human activity. It does not mean desert sand dunes spreading only. Causes: overgrazing, deforestation, bad irrigation (salinity and waterlogging), shifting cultivation, mining and climate change. Soil erosion by water is the biggest single process in India, followed by wind erosion and salinity.
The Convention

The UN Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted in Paris in 1994 and came into force in 1996 . It is one of the three Rio Conventions with the CBD and UNFCCC. Its Secretariat is in Bonn . India ratified it in 1996. The convention stresses a bottom-up approach and national action programmes. At Rio+20, the world agreed to aim for a land-degradation-neutral world. SDG 15.3 targets Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) by 2030: loss of healthy land balanced by restoration.
India's role

India hosted UNCCD COP14 at Greater Noida in September 2019 , with the theme "Restore land, sustain future". The Delhi Declaration came out of it. India raised its restoration pledge from 21 to 26 million hectares by 2030 . India held the COP presidency until COP15 (Abidjan, 2022) and has the Centre of Excellence at the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE) in Dehradun for LDN. The 2019 COP also launched a Peace Forest Initiative .
How much land is degraded

The Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas (ISRO's Space Applications Centre, 2021, for 2018-19) said about 97.85 million hectares , about 29.7 percent of India's land, is degraded. The most affected states include Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Jharkhand, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Ladakh. Water erosion is the leading process, followed by vegetation degradation and wind erosion. The Thar Desert, the Rann of Kutch and the cold desert of Ladakh are key arid zones.
What works

Afforestation and shelterbelts; the Aravalli Green Wall idea mirrors the African Great Green Wall (Sahel). Soil conservation: contour bunding, terracing, check dams, and no-till farming. Watershed programmes: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (watershed development), earlier IWMP. Soil Health Card scheme (2015). Green India Mission , MGNREGA works on land and water. Agroforestry and rotational grazing. Ravine reclamation in Chambal and sand-dune stabilisation in Rajasthan are classic examples. The Indira Gandhi Canal greened parts of the Thar but caused waterlogging in places.
Greening or grassland?

Some drylands are native open grasslands, and tree planting there harms them. The "wasteland" label invites diversion for solar parks and mines. Critics say restoration should focus on natural ecosystems, not just tree cover. Another dispute is whether farm subsidies for water and fertiliser drive salinity.
Policy links

LDN is linked to the Bonn Challenge , the Green India Mission and NDC targets (a carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes by 2030). The Central Arid Zone Research Institute (CAZRI) at Jodhpur studies arid lands. Efforts like soil carbon , natural farming and Mission LiFE link land to climate.
Quick table

UNCCD: 1994 Paris; in force 1996; Bonn. COP14: Greater Noida, 2019. Pledge: 26 million ha by 2030. SDG 15.3: LDN. Degraded land: about 29.7 percent (2018-19). Also remember that UNCCD is one of the three Rio Conventions, with the CBD and UNFCCC, and that its Secretariat sits in Bonn.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "Where was UNCCD COP14 held?" (Greater Noida). "Which Rio Convention addresses desertification?" (UNCCD). Mains-style: "What is Land Degradation Neutrality? Examine India's progress." Structure: define; scale (97.85 million ha); causes; UNCCD and COP14; Indian programmes; challenges; way forward. Use the 97.85 million hectare figure and the 26 million hectare pledge together in a conclusion.
Climate Change: Science and the Greenhouse Effect
The spine of the syllabus

Climate change links to agriculture, water, energy, security and diplomacy. UPSC asks the science in Prelims and the policy in Mains. A sound base here makes the next eight lessons easy. Always use the latest numbers and date them. The topic also connects with geography, such as the monsoon and glaciers, and with economy through energy and agriculture. UPSC asks the basic science, such as the gases, global warming potential and feedbacks, in Prelims. Mains asks for India's position, adaptation and finance. Use IPCC reports as the standard source for evidence, and give the year.
The natural greenhouse effect

Sunlight warms Earth. Earth sends heat back as long-wave radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb some of it and re-emit it, keeping the planet about 33 °C warmer than it would be. This is natural and needed for life. The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect : humans have added gases since the industrial era. Greenhouse gases are transparent to incoming short-wave sunlight but absorb outgoing long-wave infrared. Without them the average surface temperature would be about minus 18 °C instead of about 15 °C. Water vapour is the strongest natural greenhouse gas, but its amount responds to temperature, so it acts as a feedback rather than a driver. Venus shows a runaway case of the effect.
GWP and the Kyoto six

The six Kyoto gases are CO2, methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), HFCs, PFCs and SF6. Global warming potential (GWP) compares them with CO2 (GWP 1). Methane is about 28 times over 100 years but lasts only about a decade. N2O is about 270 times. SF6 is over 23,000 times. Water vapour is the biggest natural greenhouse gas but responds to temperature rather than driving it. Black carbon is a short-lived warming agent, not a gas.
The numbers

The IPCC (set up in 1988 by WMO and UNEP) reported in its Sixth Assessment (2021–23) that human activity has warmed the planet by about 1.1 °C above 1850–1900 levels. CO2 now stands above 420 ppm versus about 280 before industry (as of 2025). The World Meteorological Organization said 2024 was the first calendar year above 1.5 °C. A single year above 1.5 °C is not the same as the Paris long-term target, which is measured over decades. Sea level rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018.
Why warming can speed up

Ice-albedo feedback : melting ice exposes dark sea or land, which absorbs more heat. Permafrost thaw releases methane. Warmer oceans hold less CO2. These loops can push the climate past tipping points such as ice-sheet collapse or Amazon dieback. Ocean acidification is a related effect: dissolved CO2 lowers pH and harms corals and shellfish.
El Niño, La Niña, IOD

El Niño warms the eastern Pacific and usually weakens the Indian monsoon. La Niña is the cool phase and usually helps it. The Indian Ocean Dipole can offset El Niño when positive. These cycles cause year-to-year swings; climate change is the long-term trend. India’s monsoon forecasts depend on these links.
Responsibility

China, the US and India are the top three emitters in recent years in absolute terms. India’s per capita emissions are about half the world average, and its cumulative share is small (under 5 percent). This is the basis of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR-RC): historic emitters should lead.
Mitigation or adaptation, and who pays

Developed countries stress cutting emissions everywhere. Developing countries stress adaptation, finance and the right to develop. Some scientists urge carbon removal and geoengineering; others warn of moral hazard. The carbon budget idea gives a fixed amount of CO2 left for a temperature target. Fair shares are the core of the dispute.
India’s position

India is highly exposed to heat, floods, monsoon swings and sea-level rise. It has set a net-zero target for 2070 and stresses equity and climate justice. India is not part of the Global Methane Pledge (2021, 30 percent cut by 2030), citing livestock and rice methane tied to livelihoods.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Explain the greenhouse effect and the evidence for human-induced climate change. Why is India vulnerable?” Structure: mechanism; gases and GWP; IPCC numbers (dated); India’s exposure; two responses. Prelims tip: Kyoto has six gases. Methane has higher GWP but shorter life than CO2. IPCC founded 1988. El Niño usually weakens the monsoon.
Impacts on India: Agriculture, Water, Coasts
India feels climate change first

With 1.4 billion people, a long coast, Himalayan glaciers and a monsoon economy, India is very exposed. UPSC Mains asks for impacts and adaptation in agriculture, water and cities. Use named events and dates in answers. India ranks among the countries most affected in global climate risk indices published by German think tanks. The impacts are linked: a hotter Himalaya and altered monsoon change river flow, which affects farms, power and cities downstream. In answers, use one event per sector, such as the 2022 heatwave for agriculture and the Kerala floods of 2018 for disasters.
Rising extremes

Heatwaves are longer and earlier. In March 2022 an early heatwave cut wheat yields in parts of the north. Cities add the heat-island effect. India’s heat action plans began with Ahmedabad in 2013. Heat also hits outdoor workers and productivity, and raises power demand. Wet-bulb temperature, which combines heat and humidity, is the real danger for people, because the body cannot cool itself by sweating when it is high. The Ahmedabad plan added early warning, cool roofs and public awareness, and the NDMA now guides state and city heat action plans. Outdoor workers, the elderly and the urban poor are most exposed.
Yield and monsoon risk

Agriculture is mostly rain-fed, so changes in the monsoon matter. Heat at grain filling cuts wheat yield. Warmer nights hurt rice. Extreme rain damages standing crops. Pests and diseases shift range. ICAR’s NICRA project studies resilient crops and the ICAR has released many climate-resilient varieties. Insurance (PMFBY) cushions losses.
