Rain-fed farming covers roughly half of India's net sown area, and its yields swing with the monsoon. Rising sea level and salinity threaten delta rice areas. Shifting sowing dates, drought-tolerant seeds, micro-irrigation and crop diversification are the main adaptations. Warmer winters also shorten the wheat season in the Indo-Gangetic plain.
Glaciers and monsoon

Himalayan glaciers feed the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra. They are retreating, first adding flows and later reducing them. Glacial lake outburst floods are a growing hazard: Kedarnath 2013, Chamoli 2021 and South Lhonak, Sikkim in October 2023. Rainfall is becoming more extreme: fewer rainy days but heavier spells. Groundwater is already overused in the north-west.
Sea level and cyclones

India has about 7,500 km of coastline. Rising seas threaten the Sundarbans, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and the Lakshadweep. Salt water enters river deltas and aquifers. Cyclones in the Arabian Sea have grown more intense. Early warning and shelters have cut deaths sharply, as in Odisha after the 1999 super cyclone. Mangroves and coral reefs are natural defences.
Urban floods and landslides

Mumbai (2005), Chennai (2015), Kerala (2018) and Wayanad landslides (2024) show rising flood and slope risk, made worse by poor drainage, wetland loss and building on hills. Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand have faced repeated cloudbursts. The Himalaya’s fragile slopes are an adaptation priority. Urban flooding is driven by concrete cover, choked drains and building on floodplains and wetlands. Chennai's 2015 floods hit areas built over lakes and marshes. Cloudbursts are sudden heavy rain over a small area, which trigger flash floods in hill states. Sponge city ideas, restored wetlands and early warning systems reduce the risk.
Wider effects

Climate change spreads vector-borne diseases, reduces labour hours and worsens food prices. It drives migration from the Sundarbans and drought belts, and stress on shared rivers adds to regional tension. The poor, women and small farmers are hit hardest. This is the equity argument India makes abroad. The IPCC's sixth assessment (2021 to 2023) flagged South Asia as highly vulnerable. Sea-level rise and cyclones put Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai at risk, and climate migration adds pressure on cities. Adaptation, insurance and social protection are needed along with emission cuts.
Adaptation versus mitigation

India’s emissions are low per person, so it argues for adaptation finance. Yet adaptation needs huge money: early warning, resilient crops, drainage and housing. Critics say too much policy is about mitigation targets while state adaptation plans lack funds and data. Adaptation is local: it means drainage in cities, resilient seeds in villages and shelters on the coast. Mitigation is global, because greenhouse gases mix in the air. Under the Paris Agreement, developed countries are expected to balance finance between both, yet most climate finance has gone to mitigation. This makes the adaptation gap a key Mains point.
Policy tools

The NAPCC (2008) has missions on agriculture, water, Himalaya and habitat. States have State Action Plans . The NDMA handles disasters under the Disaster Management Act 2005. The Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (2019) was launched by India. The National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change gives limited money. India submitted its updated NDC in 2026 with adaptation themes (see lesson on NDCs). Adaptation is funded mostly by state and national budgets. The Disaster Management Act 2005 sets up the NDMA nationally and State Disaster Management Authorities in states, and the National Disaster Response Force handles response. Early cyclone warnings from the IMD have cut deaths sharply, as in Cyclone Phailin in Odisha in 2013.
How to answer

Mains-style: “How is climate change affecting Indian agriculture? Suggest adaptation measures.” Structure: heat, water and monsoon; crop examples (wheat 2022); regional pattern; adaptation (resilient seeds, micro-irrigation, insurance, crop advisories); finance and extension gaps. Mains-style: “Glacial lake outburst floods in the Himalaya: causes and mitigation.” Prelims tip: GLOF events: Kedarnath 2013, Chamoli 2021, South Lhonak 2023. CDRI launched by India in 2019.
El Nino, La Nina, IOD and the Himalayan Cryosphere
Monsoon, glaciers and floods

Climate drivers like El Nino and the Indian Ocean Dipole decide whether the monsoon fails or floods, and so decide farm output and prices. The Himalayan glaciers feed the great rivers. Prelims asks about definitions and effects. Mains asks about impacts and adaptation. Learn the two ocean systems and then the glacier story.
El Nino and La Nina

ENSO (El Nino-Southern Oscillation) is a cycle in the Pacific. In normal years, trade winds push warm water west, and cold water rises off Peru (the Walker circulation ). In an El Nino , trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east, and the Peruvian coast warms. Rain shifts east, and Indonesia and India often turn dry. In La Nina , trade winds strengthen and the eastern Pacific cools. India usually gets good monsoon rain. A year is called El Nino when the sea surface temperature in the Nino 3.4 region stays 0.5 °C above normal for several months. The cycle repeats every 2 to 7 years. The Southern Oscillation Index measures the pressure difference between Tahiti and Darwin.
What happens in India

El Nino years, such as 2009, 2014, 2015 and 2023, saw weak or deficient monsoon rain, drought risk and higher food prices. Not every El Nino brings a drought, because the Indian Ocean also matters. El Nino also raises global temperatures, and 2023 was a record-warm year. La Nina years bring more rain, floods in the north-east and colder winters in the north. Farm output, power demand and inflation respond. The IMD and the Ministry of Earth Sciences watch ENSO closely in its monsoon forecasts.
Indian Ocean Dipole

The Indian Ocean Dipole (also the Indian Nino) is the difference in sea surface temperature between the western and eastern Indian Ocean. A positive IOD (warm west, cool east) favours good Indian monsoon rain and can offset El Nino, as in 1997. A negative IOD can reduce rain. EQUINOO (the Equatorial Indian Ocean Oscillation) is a related wind pattern. The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is an eastward-moving pulse of cloud and rain that causes active and break spells of the monsoon in 30 to 60 days. A good monsoon needs a good mix of ENSO, IOD and MJO.
Himalayan glaciers

The Hindu Kush Himalaya is called the Third Pole because it has the largest ice mass outside the poles. Major glaciers include Gangotri , Siachen (one of the longest outside the poles), Zemu and Pindari. Glaciers feed the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra . Many are retreating faster this century, with black carbon and warming as causes. Hazards: Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) . Examples: Kedarnath 2013 , Chamoli 2021 (a rock and ice avalanche in the Rishiganga valley) and South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, October 2023 . Permafrost thaw destabilises slopes.
Water and tipping points

In the short term, glacier melt raises river flow, then flow falls once the ice mass is gone ("peak water"). Snow cover, not just glaciers, matters for the Indus basin. India's hill states face more landslides, and the Joshimath subsidence (2023) was a warning. Tipping points under study include the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) , ice sheets and Amazon dieback. Arctic amplification warms the north faster than the rest of the world.
Natural cycle or climate change?

ENSO is a natural cycle, but a warmer world may make El Ninos stronger. Glacier response is mixed: some Karakoram glaciers are stable or growing (the Karakoram anomaly). Critics of dam building in fragile zones say development has outrun science, while states want hydropower and roads. A balanced answer: improve forecasts, early warning and land-use planning in the mountains.
Policy tools

The National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem (NMSHE) under NAPCC, and the National Mission on Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change , study these issues. The Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (Goa) monitor ice. Mission Mausam (2024) improves weather forecasting. India runs research stations in Antarctica (Maitri, Bharati) and in the Arctic (Himadri, Svalbard).
Quick table

El Nino: warm eastern Pacific; weak monsoon likely. La Nina: cool eastern Pacific; good monsoon. Positive IOD: helps monsoon. GLOF events: 2013, 2021, 2023. Himalaya: the Third Pole. Also keep the mechanism in one line: weak trade winds, warm east Pacific, shifted rain, weaker Indian monsoon. A single mechanism line often earns the mark.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "El Nino is characterised by" (warming of the central and eastern Pacific, weakened trade winds). "Positive IOD usually leads to" (good monsoon). Mains-style: "How do El Nino and the Indian Ocean Dipole affect the Indian monsoon? Discuss adaptation." Structure: mechanism of each; combined effects; examples of years; farm and economy impact; forecasting and crop planning.
UNFCCC, Kyoto and the Paris Agreement
Treaty facts are Prelims and Mains staples

UPSC asks for the year, the principle and the difference between Kyoto and Paris. Mains asks if the system is fair and working. Master the timeline and the three principles: CBDR-RC, precaution, sustainable development.
The framework, 1992

Adopted at the Rio Earth Summit (1992) and in force from 21 March 1994 . Nearly all countries (about 198 parties) have joined. It states the goal of stabilising greenhouse gases at a safe level. The COP is its supreme body and meets yearly. Annex I lists developed countries and economies in transition. Annex II lists rich countries that must give finance and technology. Others are non-Annex I , including India and China.
Top-down targets

Adopted in 1997 , in force 2005 . Only Annex I countries had legally binding targets: about 5 percent below 1990 levels in the first period (2008–12). The Doha Amendment (2012) set a second period for 2013–20. Flexible tools: emissions trading , Joint Implementation and the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM). The US never ratified; Canada withdrew in 2011. Kyoto covered a shrinking share of global emissions.
Steps in between

Bali Action Plan (2007). Copenhagen (2009): the $100 billion a year pledge and the 2 °C goal, but not binding. Cancun (2010): Green Climate Fund created. Durban (2011): talks for a new universal deal. Lima (2014): intended nationally determined contributions (INDCs). After Kyoto, talks stalled on who should cut emissions. The Bali Action Plan opened a two-track negotiation, and Copenhagen was seen as a failure because the accord was only noted. Cancun brought its pledges into the UN process, including the Green Climate Fund. Durban started the platform that led to Paris, and Lima asked every country to submit its contribution before Paris.
Adopted 2015

Adopted on 12 December 2015 at COP21 and in force on 4 November 2016 . It is universal and legally binding on process, not on targets. Goal: keep warming well below 2 °C , pursue 1.5 °C , reach peak and then balance of sources and sinks in the second half of the century, and align finance. Each country sets its own Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and renews it every five years with a ratchet (no backsliding). Unlike Kyoto's top-down targets, Paris is bottom-up. Its transparency framework requires countries to report emissions and progress. A global stocktake happens every five years, and the first was completed at COP28 in 2023. Article 6 covers carbon markets, Article 8 recognises loss and damage, and Article 9 sets finance duties, with developed countries asked to lead.
Key articles

Article 6 : carbon markets and cooperative approaches. Rules were finalised at COP29 (Baku, 2024). Article 7 : global goal on adaptation. Article 8 : loss and damage. Article 9 : finance from developed countries. Article 13 : enhanced transparency framework. Article 14 : Global Stocktake every five years. The first ended at COP28 (2023).
Rulebook and review

The Katowice rulebook (COP24, 2018) set the detailed rules. COP26 Glasgow (2021) asked countries to revisit targets and agreed to phase down unabated coal. The Global Stocktake concluded at COP28 (Dubai, 2023) and called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems. By 2025 countries were due to submit new NDCs for 2035. Many were late, and India filed its updated NDC in 2026.
Kyoto versus Paris

Kyoto was top-down, binding for rich countries only, but limited in reach. Paris is bottom-up and universal, but targets are voluntary and current pledges still point beyond 2 °C without more action. The US formally left Paris with effect from January 2026 (second time), which weakens finance. Developing countries say CBDR-RC has been diluted.
India’s stand

India ratified Paris in October 2016. It insists on equity, CBDR-RC, a historic responsibility link, climate finance and technology transfer. It supports market mechanisms with safeguards and opposes unilateral carbon border taxes such as the EU’s CBAM. India’s net-zero target is 2070, announced at COP26 (2021).
How to answer

Mains-style: “Compare the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement. Which is better for India?” Structure: Kyoto top-down, only Annex I; Paris bottom-up, NDCs; equity and finance; India’s gains (flexibility, space to develop) and risks (pressure to raise targets, CBAM). Mains-style: “CBDR-RC: is it being diluted?” Prelims tip: UNFCCC adopted 1992, in force 1994. Kyoto adopted 1997, in force 2005. Paris adopted 2015, in force 2016. CDM is under Kyoto’s Article 12.
COPs and Climate Finance
COP outcomes are the most current part of the paper

UPSC asks about the latest COP, the finance goal and India’s position. These answers must carry names, numbers and years. As of 2026: COP30 (Belém, Brazil) ended in November 2025. COP31 is due in Antalya, Türkiye in November 2026 as this lesson is written, so check its outcome.
What a COP is

The Conference of the Parties is the supreme body of the UNFCCC. It meets every year. A Presidency (host country) steers talks, and decisions are by consensus. The Subsidiary Bodies (SBSTA, SBI) prepare technical work. Alongside it, the CMA governs the Paris Agreement. The COP presidency rotates among the five UN regional groups. Decisions need consensus, which means that a single objecting party can slow talks. Observers include NGOs and business groups. The UNFCCC secretariat is in Bonn, and the first COP was held in Berlin in 1995. COP3 produced the Kyoto Protocol in 1997, and COP21 in Paris produced the Paris Agreement.
Dubai 2023 and Baku 2024

COP28 (Dubai): the first Global Stocktake called for transitioning away from fossil fuels , tripling renewable capacity to 11,000 GW and doubling efficiency by 2030. The Loss and Damage Fund was launched on day one. COP29 (Baku): the New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) set $300 billion a year by 2035 from developed countries, within a wider aim of $1.3 trillion a year from all sources. India called the offer inadequate. Article 6 carbon market rules were also settled. Dubai gave direction and Baku gave money. The stocktake judged that countries were off track for the 1.5 °C goal. The Loss and Damage Fund is hosted by the World Bank as an interim arrangement. At Baku, developing countries said the finance sum was far below need, and India objected at the closing plenary.
Belém 2025

COP30 was held in Belém, Brazil, in the Amazon. It ended with the Global Mutirão decision. Main results: a call to triple adaptation finance by 2035 (without a clear base year), voluntary Belém adaptation indicators , a Just Transition mechanism, a two-year work programme on climate finance and a push to speed up implementation. The text did not name a roadmap to end fossil fuels, and deforestation had no roadmap in the final text. Brazil promised to prepare voluntary roadmaps. The Tropical Forests Forever Facility was launched with pledges from some countries.
Positions

India stressed equity, CBDR-RC and finance, and opposed unilateral trade measures like the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) , whose definitive phase began in January 2026. It supported adaptation finance and a just transition. India argued that developed countries must deliver the earlier $100 billion promise and scale it up before asking developing countries to do more.
Antalya 2026

Türkiye will host COP31 in Antalya in November 2026. Under a compromise, Australia leads the negotiations as President of the negotiations, and a pre-COP in the Pacific is planned (as of 2026, reports; verify final arrangements). Watch for the 2035 NDC gap, the finance work programme, adaptation indicators and the fossil fuel roadmap.
The architecture

Global Environment Facility (1991): finances UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD work. Green Climate Fund (Cancun 2010, Songdo, South Korea): the largest dedicated fund. Adaptation Fund (under Kyoto). Loss and Damage Fund (operational from COP28; hosted by the World Bank). LDCF and SCCF for least developed countries.
Delivery

Copenhagen (2009) promised $100 billion a year by 2020. The OECD reported it was first met in 2022. Developing countries dispute how loans are counted and how much is grant. The NCQG replaces it from 2025, but the $300 billion figure is far below the $1.3 trillion need, and much will be loans.
Mitigation versus adaptation finance

Most money goes to mitigation, such as solar. Adaptation gets less and loss and damage the least. Climate finance is also seen as debt creation for poor countries. Rich countries say public money is limited and private capital must be mobilised. Developing countries want public grants.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Climate finance is the real test of Paris. Examine the gaps and India’s position.” Structure: needs; promise ($100 billion, NCQG $300 billion); gaps (loans, accounting, adaptation); India’s demand (grants, CBDR, no CBAM); way forward (reform of MDBs, Article 6, carbon markets). Prelims tip: GCF from Cancun 2010, HQ in Songdo. NCQG is $300 billion by 2035. COP28 Dubai started the Loss and Damage Fund.
Ozone, Montreal Protocol and Other Conventions
Convention names and years are free marks

Prelims often matches a convention with its subject or year. The Montreal Protocol is also the most cited success story in global environmental governance. Learn the ozone chain, then the table of conventions. Prelims often tests pairs such as Basel with hazardous waste, Ramsar with wetlands, and Minamata with mercury. Build a timeline in your head: 1971 Ramsar, 1972 Stockholm and World Heritage, 1973 CITES, 1987 Montreal, 1992 Rio. Also remember that Vienna is the framework and Montreal is the protocol with binding limits.
What and where

Ozone (O3) in the stratosphere (peak about 20 to 30 km up) absorbs harmful UV-B and UV-C. It is measured in Dobson Units . Ground-level ozone is a pollutant. Rowland and Molina (1974) warned about CFCs. In 1985 Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin reported the Antarctic ozone hole. Crutzen, Rowland and Molina won the Nobel Prize in 1995. UV-B can cause skin cancer, cataracts and damage to crops and plankton. The ozone hole forms over Antarctica each spring (September to October) because polar stratospheric clouds help chlorine destroy ozone. Remember the contrast: stratospheric ozone is protective, while tropospheric (ground-level) ozone is a pollutant.
Chlorine chain

CFCs are stable, drift up, and in the stratosphere UV frees chlorine. One chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. The hole forms in the Antarctic spring (September to October) because polar stratospheric clouds help the reaction. Other ozone depleting substances (ODS): halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, methyl bromide, HCFCs.
The treaties

The Vienna Convention (1985) set up cooperation. The Montreal Protocol (1987, in force 1989) phases out ODS. It is the first treaty ratified by every country in the world. It works with a Multilateral Fund to help developing countries, and has binding timetables. Amendments: London (1990), Copenhagen (1992), Montreal (1997), Beijing (1999) and Kigali (2016) .
HFCs

HFCs do not harm ozone but are strong greenhouse gases. The Kigali Amendment (in force 2019) phases them down. India ratified it in 2021. India’s schedule: freeze in 2028 and cuts in steps, with an 85 percent reduction by 2047, later than developed countries. Scientists project the ozone layer recovering by about 2040 (most of the world), 2045 (Arctic) and 2066 (Antarctic), per UNEP’s 2022 assessment.
Biodiversity and land

Ramsar 1971: wetlands. World Heritage Convention 1972. CITES 1973: trade in endangered species. CMS 1979 (Bonn): migratory species. CBD 1992 with Cartagena Protocol (2000, biosafety) and Nagoya Protocol (2010, access and benefit sharing). UNCCD 1994: desertification. The Ramsar and World Heritage conventions protect sites, while CITES and CMS protect species. CBD, adopted at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, has three goals: conservation, sustainable use and fair sharing of benefits. Its Kunming-Montreal framework of 2022 sets global biodiversity goals. UNCCD, also born at Rio, is the only legally binding convention on land.
Chemicals and seas

Basel 1989: hazardous waste. Rotterdam 1998: prior informed consent for chemicals. Stockholm 2001: persistent organic pollutants. Minamata 2013: mercury (in force 2017). MARPOL 1973/78: ship pollution. BBNJ (High Seas Treaty), adopted 2023 and in force from January 2026. The Basel Convention covers cross-border movement of hazardous waste. Rotterdam and Stockholm deal with hazardous pesticides and persistent organic pollutants such as DDT. Minamata is named after the Japanese city where mercury poisoning was seen in the 1950s. MARPOL has six annexes covering oil, chemicals, sewage, garbage and air pollution from ships. BBNJ concerns biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction.
Why did Montreal work?

Success factors: clear science, substitutes available, binding timetables, trade restrictions on non-parties, a fund for poor countries and a review system. Climate change is harder: no easy substitute for fossil fuels, costs are high and benefits are shared. Some argue the Kigali style phase-down model could help other gases. Montreal's Multilateral Fund helped developing countries pay for the switch, and longer timetables gave India and China more time, reflecting common but differentiated responsibilities. The treaty has been amended several times (London, Copenhagen, Montreal, Beijing and Kigali) so it adjusts to new science. It was the first treaty ratified by every country.
India’s record

India phased out CFCs by 2010 and has a Ozone Cell in MoEFCC and an HCFC Phase-out Management Plan. India is a party to all the conventions above. India submitted its 2022 and 2026 climate plans and hosted CMS COP13 (2020) and UNCCD COP14 (2019).
How to answer

Mains-style: “Montreal Protocol is the most successful environmental treaty. What lessons does it offer for climate change?” Structure: what it did; why it worked; limits of the analogy; Kigali; India’s role. Prelims tip: Montreal = ozone, 1987. Kigali = HFCs. Basel = hazardous waste. Minamata = mercury. Rotterdam = PIC chemicals.
IPCC Reports, Carbon Budget and Net Zero
The science behind talks

IPCC findings are cited in almost every climate question. Prelims asks about its structure and key numbers. Mains asks about net zero, carbon budgets and how science shapes policy. This lesson sets out the institution, the reports and the terms. Expect statement questions mixing the IPCC with the UNFCCC, so remember that the IPCC assesses science and does not negotiate.
What the IPCC is

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was set up in 1988 by the WMO and UNEP . It does not do new research. It assesses published science for governments. Its reports are approved line by line by member governments, so they are "policy relevant, not policy prescriptive". It shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize with Al Gore. There are three working groups: WG I (physical science), WG II (impacts, adaptation, vulnerability) and WG III (mitigation), plus a task force on national inventories. The Secretariat is in Geneva.
Assessment cycles

The Assessment Reports (AR) come every 6 to 7 years. AR6 was released in 2021-23. The AR6 Synthesis Report (March 2023) said human activity has caused about 1.1 °C of warming above 1850-1900 levels. Special reports include the Special Report on 1.5 °C (2018) , which said limiting warming to 1.5 °C needs cuts of about 45 percent in CO2 by 2030 from 2010 levels and net zero around 2050 . The AR7 cycle began in 2023. The UNEP Emissions Gap Report is a different yearly report that compares promises with the needed path.
How much more can we emit

A carbon budget is the total CO2 the world can still release for a given chance of staying below a temperature limit. AR6 put the remaining budget for 1.5 °C at around 500 gigatonnes of CO2 from early 2020 for a 50 percent chance. Current emissions are about 40 gigatonnes a year, so the budget is used up within roughly a decade at the current pace. Global warming potential (GWP) compares gases to CO2 over 100 years: methane about 28 times (AR5/AR6 range) and nitrous oxide about 265 times.
Terms to separate

Net zero: emissions into the air are balanced by removals from the air. Carbon neutral: a similar idea, often used for products or firms. Carbon sink: forests, soils, oceans, which absorb CO2. Carbon removal: direct air capture, afforestation, BECCS. Overshoot: temporarily exceeding 1.5 °C, then removing carbon. India's target is net zero by 2070 , announced at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021). China aims for 2060 and the EU for 2050. About 140 countries have net zero pledges.
Pathways and shared stories

AR6 uses Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) , which tie social choices to emissions, replacing the earlier RCPs (Representative Concentration Pathways). A low pathway needs fast cuts, while a high one leads to above 3 to 4 °C. Climate tipping points and compound extremes get more attention in AR6. The Paris Agreement goal is well below 2 °C, aiming at 1.5 °C.
Is net zero credible?

Critics say net zero pledges depend on future removal technologies that are not proven at scale and may serve as an excuse to delay action. Developing countries say rich nations should reach net zero earlier, because of their historical emissions. Another point is that offsets can hide real emissions. A fair view: net zero by mid-century is needed, but only after deep cuts that come first.
India in the IPCC and net zero

India is among the largest emitters in total but is low in per-capita and historical emissions (about 4 percent of cumulative CO2). Indian scientists have served as lead authors, and R.K. Pachauri chaired the IPCC (2002-15) when it won the Nobel. India stresses climate equity and the idea of a carbon budget shared fairly. Its Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS) was submitted at COP27 (2022).
Numbers table

IPCC: 1988, WMO and UNEP. Warming so far: about 1.1 °C (AR6). 1.5 °C budget: about 500 Gt CO2 from 2020. India net zero: 2070. Special Report 1.5 °C: 2018. Hold also: AR6 in 2021-23, Synthesis Report in March 2023, and a 45 percent cut in CO2 by 2030 for 1.5 degrees.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "IPCC was established by" (WMO and UNEP). "India's net zero target year is" (2070). Mains-style: "What is the carbon budget approach? Examine India's net zero commitment." Structure: define budget; global figures; equity and history; India's 2070 goal and Panchamrit; mitigation steps; critique and way forward.
Climate Justice: CBDR, Loss and Damage, Stocktake
Fairness is the core fight

Almost every climate negotiation is a fight over fairness: who caused the problem, who pays and who adapts. Prelims asks about CBDR, Annexes and funds. Mains asks you to argue India's case. The key terms are CBDR-RC, climate finance, the Loss and Damage Fund and the Global Stocktake.
Common but differentiated responsibilities

CBDR comes from Principle 7 of the Rio Declaration (1992) and Article 3 of the UNFCCC. All states share a common duty to protect the climate, but their duties differ because they contributed differently and have different capacity. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) divided states into Annex I (developed countries, with binding targets) and non-Annex I . The Paris Agreement (2015) moved to nationally determined contributions (NDCs) from all, and added "in the light of different national circumstances" (CBDR-RC). India and China insist on keeping the differentiation.
Climate finance and the $100 billion

At Copenhagen (2009), developed countries promised US$100 billion a year by 2020. It was reached late, and the OECD said it was met in 2022. The Green Climate Fund (set up at Cancun 2010; HQ Songdo, South Korea) is the main fund. The Adaptation Fund and GEF also work. At COP29 (Baku, 2024) , a New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) set US$300 billion a year by 2035 from developed countries, within a wider aim of US$1.3 trillion from all sources. India called the figure too low.
The new fund

Loss and damage means harm from climate change that adaptation cannot avoid, like island loss or flood damage. The Warsaw International Mechanism (2013) began the work. At COP27 (Sharm el-Sheikh, 2022) , countries agreed to set up a fund. At COP28 (Dubai, 2023) it was made operational on day one, with initial pledges of about US$700 million. The World Bank hosts it as an interim step. The Santiago Network gives technical help. Small island states and the least developed countries pushed for this for decades.
Global Stocktake

Article 14 of the Paris Agreement requires a Global Stocktake (GST) every five years to measure collective progress. The first GST ended at COP28 (2023) with a call to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems , the first time such wording entered a COP decision. It also called for tripling renewable energy capacity and doubling energy efficiency by 2030. Countries will submit new NDCs by 2025 informed by it. COP26 (Glasgow 2021) had agreed to phase down unabated coal, a wording India and China changed from "phase out".
India's arguments

India says rich countries used up much of the carbon budget. India's per-capita emissions are about 2 tonnes of CO2 , far below the US and EU (figures vary by year). It argues for climate equity , technology transfer and finance, and opposes unilateral trade measures like the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) , which taxes carbon in imports from 2026. India also pushes LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment, 2021) as a demand-side idea.
Who is a developing country now?

The Annex lists of 1992 are old. China is the largest emitter today, and Gulf states are rich. Developed countries say big emitters must pay. Poorer states say historical responsibility remains. The BASIC group (Brazil, South Africa, India, China) and the Like-Minded Developing Countries hold the line on differentiation, while the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) wants faster cuts.
Positions and results

India submitted its updated NDC in August 2022 (45 percent cut in emissions intensity from 2005 levels and 50 percent non-fossil power capacity by 2030) and announced Panchamrit at COP26. At COP28 India did not sign the pledge to triple renewable capacity, citing the need to treat all energy sources and equity fairly.
Quick table

CBDR: Rio 1992, Principle 7. $100 bn: Copenhagen 2009. GCF: Cancun 2010, Songdo. Loss and Damage Fund: agreed COP27 2022; operational COP28 2023. GST: Article 14; first at COP28. NCQG: COP29, $300 bn by 2035. Also hold: COP26 Glasgow 2021 for Panchamrit and coal phase down; COP28 Dubai 2023 for the stocktake.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "CBDR principle was first recognised in" (Rio Declaration 1992). "The Green Climate Fund is headquartered in" (Songdo). Mains-style: "Explain climate justice and India's stand on climate finance." Structure: history and CBDR; finance gaps; loss and damage; GST; India's per-capita and historical argument; CBAM; way forward.
International Solar Alliance, CDRI and Global Initiatives
India as a leader of coalitions

India has started several global groups in the last decade. Prelims asks where they are headquartered and when they began. Mains asks whether such soft power gets results. A table of name, year, aim and HQ is the best way to revise.
International Solar Alliance

The International Solar Alliance (ISA) was launched by India and France at COP21, Paris, on 30 November 2015 . Its HQ is at Gurugram , Haryana, hosted on the NIWE campus. The Framework Agreement came into force in December 2017 , making ISA a treaty-based international organisation. It works with the "sunshine countries" between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn . A 2020 amendment opened membership to all UN member states. Its aim is to mobilise US$1 trillion by 2030 for solar and to cut costs. The slogan is "One Sun, One World, One Grid".
One Sun One World One Grid

OSOWOG was announced by PM Modi at the first ISA Assembly (2018) and elaborated at COP26 (2021) as a Green Grids Initiative with the UK. It would link solar-rich areas across regions by cross-border grids, so that the sun is always shining somewhere to feed demand. Phases include India to Gulf and Southeast Asia, then to Africa, then a global grid. Its backers say it cuts costs and storage needs.
Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure

CDRI was launched by India at the UN Climate Action Summit, New York, in September 2019 . The Secretariat is in New Delhi . It helps countries build roads, power and telecom that survive hazards, and it supports small island developing states. It is a partnership of national governments, UN agencies, multilateral banks and the private sector. It links to the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030) , adopted at the UN conference in Sendai, Japan, in 2015.
Quick list

LeadIT (Leadership Group for Industry Transition, 2019): India and Sweden, heavy industry decarbonisation. Global Biofuels Alliance (2023): launched at the G20 in New Delhi, to promote biofuels such as ethanol. International Big Cat Alliance (2023): Mysuru, seven big cats. Mission LiFE (2022): Lifestyle for Environment, launched with the UN Secretary-General. Mangrove Alliance for Climate (COP27, UAE and Indonesia), which India joined. Global Methane Pledge (2021): India did not sign it.
Solar at home

India's solar targets: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030. The National Solar Mission (2010, under NAPCC) started at 20 GW by 2022, later raised to 100 GW and met around 2024-25 (check the latest). The PM-KUSUM scheme (2019) helps farmers with solar pumps. The PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (2024) targets rooftop solar for 1 crore homes . Bhadla (Rajasthan) is among the world's largest solar parks.
Soft power or substance?

Supporters say the alliances lift India's global role and tie finance to Indian ideas. Critics say ISA has raised smaller money than promised, and India's own solar manufacturing depends on Chinese imports. Dependence on imported cells and modules is a vulnerability, and the PLI scheme for solar modules tries to reduce it.
Why India leads

India is among the top three solar markets. Its credibility rests on cheap solar auctions, rooftop growth and a large target. The ISA's headquarters in India and the CDRI secretariat in Delhi give India agenda-setting power in the Global South.
Table to memorise

ISA: 2015 Paris; HQ Gurugram; treaty in force 2017. CDRI: 2019 New York; Secretariat Delhi. LeadIT: 2019; Sweden and India. Global Biofuels Alliance: 2023 G20. IBCA: 2023 Mysuru. Sendai Framework: 2015-30.
How to answer

Prelims-style: "The International Solar Alliance is headquartered at" (Gurugram). "CDRI was launched at" (UN Climate Action Summit, 2019). Mains-style: "Examine India's role in building global climate coalitions." Structure: ISA, CDRI, LeadIT, GBA; aims and results; domestic base (solar capacity); criticisms; way forward.
NAPCC, Missions and India’s NDCs
India’s own plan is the core of GS-III climate

Questions ask for the eight NAPCC missions, the targets of the NDC, the five-point Panchamrit and net-zero 2070. The newest NDC was filed in 2026, so recent facts matter. Always say which NDC you mean: 2015, 2022 or the 2031–35 update. Questions often ask what India has promised, when, and how well it is doing. A clean timeline helps: NAPCC 2008, first NDC 2015, Panchamrit 2021, update 2022 and a further update after that. Use a table in your answer with target, year and baseline. Remember that targets for emission intensity use 2005 as the baseline year.
June 2008

The National Action Plan on Climate Change has eight missions: Solar , Enhanced Energy Efficiency , Sustainable Habitat , Water , Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem , Green India , Sustainable Agriculture , and Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change . States prepare State Action Plans on Climate Change (SAPCC) . Critics say the missions got uneven funding and weak monitoring. The Solar mission (Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission, 2010) later raised its target to 100 GW by 2022, which was not met on time. The Enhanced Energy Efficiency mission created the PAT scheme (Perform, Achieve and Trade). Green India aims to expand and improve forest cover. The Prime Minister's Council on Climate Change oversees the plan.
Paris pledge

Cut emission intensity of GDP by 33 to 35 percent by 2030 from 2005. 40 percent of installed electric capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030. Create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2e through forests. India's first pledge was among the most carefully balanced: an emission intensity target, a non-fossil capacity target and a forest carbon sink. The Intended Nationally Determined Contribution was submitted in October 2015 before the Paris conference, and became India's first NDC when India ratified the agreement in October 2016. The 2022 update later raised the intensity target from 33 to 35 percent up to 45 percent.
Panchamrit

At COP26 (2021) , India announced: 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50 percent of energy needs from renewables by 2030; cut projected emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030; cut emission intensity by 45 percent ; and net-zero by 2070 . The updated NDC (August 2022) raised the targets: 45 percent intensity cut and 50 percent non-fossil electric capacity by 2030. India reached 50 percent non-fossil installed capacity in mid-2025, about five years early. Panchamrit means five nectars. The intensity target is measured against GDP, not as an absolute cap, with 2005 as the baseline. India's stance rests on equity and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC): developed countries should provide finance and technology. India calls this climate justice and stresses its low per capita emissions.
The 2031–35 pledge

The Cabinet approved India’s new NDC in March 2026 for submission to the UNFCCC. Reports state two headline goals: at least 47 percent cut in the emission intensity of GDP from 2005 levels by 2035 and about 60 percent non-fossil electric capacity by 2035. It also aims for an extra carbon sink of 3.5 to 4 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through forests by 2035. India filed after most G20 members and long after the September 2025 expected date. The target is an intensity goal, not an absolute cap on emissions.
Strategy and alliances

India’s Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy was submitted at COP27 (2022). The International Solar Alliance (2015, HQ Gurugram) and CDRI (2019) are Indian-led. Mission LiFE (2022) promotes sustainable lifestyles. India’s climate finance need is estimated in trillions of dollars, and it argues most must come from developed countries.
Targets met and missed

India’s emission intensity fell by about 33 percent between 2005 and 2019, according to its reporting to the UNFCCC, and non-fossil capacity targets have been met early. The forest carbon sink target is harder: the 2.5 to 3 billion tonne goal depends on forest quality and plantation survival. Absolute emissions are still rising with the economy, which is why the intensity form of the target draws comment.
Is India doing enough?

Supporters point to rapid solar growth, early targets met and low per capita emissions. Critics note that coal still dominates power, intensity targets allow absolute emissions to rise, and the 2070 net-zero date is later than many. India says it is doing its fair share and that finance, not ambition, is the gap.
Institutions

The MoEFCC is the nodal ministry. The Prime Minister’s Council on Climate Change oversees. Missions are run by ministries: MNRE (solar), BEE (energy efficiency), Ministry of Jal Shakti (water). Bureau of Energy Efficiency runs the PAT scheme, now being replaced by carbon trading. State governments prepare State Action Plans, and local bodies carry out adaptation. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency, under the Ministry of Power, runs PAT, which trades energy-saving certificates among large industries. The new carbon market is designed to take over from it. The International Solar Alliance, launched by India and France in 2015, is headquartered in Gurugram.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Critically examine India’s updated NDC. Is it consistent with equity and ambition?” Structure: targets (give years); progress (50 percent non-fossil capacity); gaps (coal, finance, intensity not cap); equity argument; way forward. Mains-style: “What are the missions under the NAPCC? How successful have they been?” Prelims tip: NAPCC 2008, eight missions. Panchamrit at COP26. LTS at COP27. ISA HQ Gurugram. Answer pointers: begin with data, not opinion. Contrast intensity targets with absolute caps. Note that 2070 is later than the 2050 date of many developed countries, but India's per capita emissions are far below the world average. Close with finance, technology transfer and a just transition for coal-dependent workers and states.
Renewable Energy and Energy Transition
Energy is the heart of India’s climate bargain

India must grow its economy, give reliable power, cut imports and shrink emissions together. UPSC asks about solar, wind, green hydrogen, nuclear and storage. Use dated numbers. The core tension is that energy demand must grow for development, while emissions must fall. Renewable sources help with both, yet their output varies, so storage and grid upgrades matter. Energy security is another driver, as India imports most of its crude oil. Mention all five choices in answers: solar, wind, hydro, nuclear and green hydrogen.
Capacity

India reached 50 percent non-fossil installed capacity in mid-2025 (about 485 GW total at the time), five years before the 2030 target. Solar crossed 100 GW in early 2025 and has kept rising (as of 2026, check MNRE). Coal still gives roughly 70 percent of the electricity generated, because solar and wind run only part of the day. Capacity is not the same as generation. Solar plants run at a capacity utilisation of roughly 20 to 25 percent, while coal plants run far higher, so a large renewable capacity gives a smaller share of electricity. Rajasthan and Gujarat lead in solar, and Tamil Nadu and Gujarat in wind. Grid integration and storage are the bottleneck.

The Glasgow goal is 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 , with solar as the largest part, then wind, hydro and nuclear. The earlier goal of 100 GW solar by 2022 was missed. At COP28, over 100 countries backed a pledge to triple renewable capacity by 2030. India did not sign the pledge text, saying it prefers its own targets and wants equity in burden sharing.
Rooftop, farms and factories

PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (2024): rooftop solar for 1 crore homes. PM-KUSUM (2019): solar pumps and feeders for farmers. PLI scheme and ALMM for domestic solar modules. Solar parks and the One Sun One World One Grid idea. The rooftop scheme gives subsidy support so that households can generate their own power and sell the surplus to the grid. PM-KUSUM has three components: stand-alone solar pumps, grid-connected pumps and solarising feeders. The ALMM list names approved solar module makers to support domestic manufacturing. India and France launched the International Solar Alliance in 2015, and the One Sun One World One Grid idea links regional grids.
National Green Hydrogen Mission

Launched in January 2023 with about ₹19,744 crore. Aim: 5 million tonnes a year of green hydrogen by 2030. Green hydrogen is made by splitting water with renewable power. It is for steel, fertiliser, refineries and shipping. Challenges: high cost, electrolyser supply and storage. The SIGHT scheme supports electrolyser and hydrogen output. Grey hydrogen comes from natural gas, and blue is grey with carbon capture. Green is the cleanest. Fertiliser and refining already use hydrogen, so the first demand exists. Pilots include hydrogen buses and trains, and hubs have been planned at ports such as Kandla, Paradip and Tuticorin.
The firm power

Nuclear gives under 3 percent now. Budget 2025–26 announced a Nuclear Energy Mission with ₹20,000 crore for small modular reactors and a goal of 100 GW by 2047, with a role for private firms. Hydropower and pumped storage give balancing. Battery storage is supported by viability gap funding. The grid needs more transmission.
Why it is hard

Intermittency needs storage. Land is scarce. Solar equipment relies on imports, mostly from China. Critical minerals (lithium, cobalt, rare earths) are needed, and India launched the National Critical Mineral Mission in 2025. Coal states such as Jharkhand and Odisha depend on mining jobs, so a just transition is vital.
Coal or clean first?

India’s power demand is growing fast, and the government continues adding coal capacity for reliability while expanding renewables. Critics worry about stranded assets and health costs. Supporters stress energy security and affordability. Another debate: large solar parks versus rooftop and community systems. Coal provides baseload power and many jobs and state revenues, while its use adds to emissions and local air pollution. Renewable energy can be built faster and is now cheaper per unit, but needs storage to supply at night. Decentralised rooftop systems cut transmission losses and give households a stake. A balanced answer shows both views and then proposes a phased, just transition.
Transport and efficiency

PM E-DRIVE (2024) supports electric vehicles after FAME II. Ethanol blending reached 20 percent in 2025, ahead of schedule. Energy efficiency is guided by the Energy Conservation Act 2001 and BEE star labels. Viksit Bharat 2047 and Net Zero 2070 frame the long path. E20 blending draws on sugarcane and grain, so critics link it to water use and food prices. Electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers and buses are the main focus of PM E-DRIVE. The BEE star label rates appliances such as air conditioners. The Energy Conservation Act 2001 created the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, and a 2022 amendment added a basis for carbon markets.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Discuss the challenges in India’s transition to renewable energy and suggest solutions.” Structure: progress (50 percent non-fossil capacity); barriers (intermittency, grid, import dependence, financing, land, coal jobs); solutions (storage, green hydrogen, domestic manufacturing, nuclear, just transition). Prelims tip: NGHM 2023, target 5 MMT. PM-KUSUM 2019. PM Surya Ghar 2024. ISA 2015. Extra points: the transition is a just transition issue for coal states such as Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh. Dependence on imported solar cells and critical minerals is a risk, and a PLI scheme for solar modules supports local manufacturing. Use examples: Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan, Pavagada in Karnataka, and Cochin airport as a solar-powered airport.
Carbon Markets, Green Credit and LiFE
New tools, new questions

India has built three connected instruments: a compliance carbon market, the Green Credit Programme and Mission LiFE. They are fresh in the news and ideal for Mains. Keep them separate in your mind: one prices carbon, one rewards land and nature actions, one changes behaviour.
How carbon markets work

A compliance market sets a legal limit or intensity target for firms. Those who beat it earn credits and sell to those who miss. A voluntary market lets firms buy credits to offset their emissions. Two designs: cap-and-trade (absolute cap, as in the EU ETS, started 2005) and baseline-and-credit (intensity targets). India uses the intensity model.
The legal base

The Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022 allowed carbon markets. The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme was notified in 2023 and its rules sit with the Ministry of Power. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency is the administrator, the Grid Controller of India is registry, and CERC regulates trading. It replaces the earlier PAT energy efficiency scheme (2012). One credit equals one tonne of CO2e.
As of 2026

Intensity targets for 2025–26 and 2026–27 have been notified in stages for energy-intensive sectors including aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp and paper , and later petroleum refining, petrochemicals, textiles and others (as of 2026; reports differ on counts of units). Targets have been notified for nine sectors (power is excluded); trading was targeted to begin around October 2026. An offset mechanism also allows non-obligated projects, such as renewables and afforestation, to earn credits.
Nature-based rewards

The Green Credit Rules were notified under the Environment Protection Act in October 2023. It is voluntary and market-based, and the administrator is ICFRE , Dehradun. At COP28 India launched the Green Credit Initiative. Eligible activities include tree plantation, water conservation, sustainable agriculture, waste management, air pollution reduction, mangrove restoration, Ecomark and sustainable building . People or firms can earn a credit and trade it.
Lifestyle for Environment

LiFE was announced by the Prime Minister at COP26 (2021) and launched on 20 October 2022 at Kevadia, Gujarat with the UN Secretary-General. It promotes simple habits: saving energy and water, cutting waste and plastic, eating sustainably and adopting healthy lifestyles. It builds Pro-Planet People and treats behaviour as a climate tool, backed by India’s case that overconsumption in rich countries is a cause.
Article 6

The Paris Agreement’s Article 6 allows international transfer of credits (6.2) and a UN-supervised crediting mechanism (6.4). Rules agreed at COP29 (2024) open the way for India’s credits to be sold abroad, with safeguards against double counting. India will need to match domestic CCTS rules with Article 6 accounting.
Risks and criticism

Carbon markets can fail through weak baselines, double counting and low prices. Intensity targets may not cap total emissions. Green Credit has been criticised for treating nature like a commodity and for land tied up in plantations. Supporters say markets mobilise private money and reward early action, and are better than rules alone.
Why it matters to India

India’s industry is energy-intensive and exports face the EU CBAM from 2026. A domestic carbon price could help exporters show they already pay a price for carbon. The three tools fit the NDC goals and the 2070 net-zero target. CBAM, the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, taxes imports of carbon-intensive goods such as steel, cement, aluminium and fertiliser, with a transition period that began in 2023 and charges that follow later. Indian exporters worry about competitiveness. A domestic carbon price may reduce the amount payable abroad. India has also objected that CBAM breaks the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What is the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme? How does it differ from PAT and from the Green Credit Programme?” Structure: definitions; legal base; sector coverage; differences (compliance versus voluntary, industry versus nature); risks; way forward. Prelims tip: CCTS: BEE as administrator. Green Credit Administrator: ICFRE. LiFE launched 2022. EU ETS began 2005. Answer pointers: the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022 gave the legal basis for a carbon market. CCTS uses emission intensity targets for covered entities, unlike absolute caps in the EU ETS. The Green Credit Programme rewards voluntary actions such as tree planting and water conservation, so it is not a compliance market. Do not mix PAT energy savings certificates with carbon credits. Mention double counting and price discovery as risks.
Environmental Laws and the NGT
Law is how environment policy bites

Prelims asks the year and subject of each Act and the NGT’s powers. Mains asks whether Indian environmental law is effective. Learn the constitutional base, the main Acts and the principles courts use. The legal map has three layers: the Constitution, the Acts and the courts. Remember the major Acts with their years: Wildlife 1972, Water 1974, Forest Conservation 1980, Air 1981, Environment Protection 1986, Biological Diversity 2002, Forest Rights 2006, NGT 2010. In Mains, discuss a gap between strong laws and weak enforcement, with an example.
Articles to remember

Article 48A (DPSP, added by the 42nd Amendment 1976): the State shall protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife. Article 51A(g) : a Fundamental Duty of every citizen. Article 21 : courts read a right to a healthy environment into the right to life (Subhash Kumar v State of Bihar, 1991). The 42nd Amendment also moved forests and wild animals to the Concurrent List (Entries 17A, 17B). Article 253 lets Parliament legislate to implement treaties. Article 253 let Parliament pass the Environment Protection Act 1986 after the Bhopal gas disaster (1984), partly to implement the Stockholm 1972 decisions. Articles 243G and the Eleventh Schedule give panchayats a role. The public trust doctrine was applied in M C Mehta v Kamal Nath (1997). Articles 32 and 226 allow writ petitions in the Supreme Court and High Courts.
Year by year

Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 Water Act 1974 ; Water Cess Act 1977 Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 Air Act 1981 Environment (Protection) Act 1986 : the umbrella law, passed after Bhopal (December 1984) and the Stockholm Conference. Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 Biological Diversity Act 2002 Forest Rights Act 2006 ; NGT Act 2010
The umbrella

It gives the Centre power to set standards, restrict industry locations, issue directions and make rules such as the EIA, CRZ, noise and waste rules. Offences carry penalties. Under the Jan Vishwas Act 2023, many jail terms in the EPA were replaced by penalties (from ₹10,000 up to ₹15 lakh), with adjudicating officers. Supporters see ease of business; critics see weaker deterrence.
Used by the courts

Polluter pays , precautionary principle and public trust doctrine were all accepted in Indian law. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum (1996) and the Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996) cases built these in. M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath (1997) applied the public trust doctrine. In M.C. Mehta (Oleum gas leak, 1986) the Court created absolute liability for hazardous industries, going beyond the old strict liability of Rylands v Fletcher.
Set up in 2010

The National Green Tribunal Act 2010 created the NGT, replacing the National Environment Tribunal (1995) and the National Environment Appellate Authority (1997). The Principal Bench is in Delhi, with benches at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai. India became one of the few countries with a specialist green tribunal. The chair is a retired Supreme Court judge or High Court Chief Justice, along with judicial and expert members.
Jurisdiction

The NGT hears civil cases involving a substantial environmental question under seven Acts: Water, Water Cess, Forest Conservation, Air, Environment Protection, Public Liability Insurance and Biological Diversity. It does not hear cases under the Wildlife Protection Act, the Indian Forest Act 1927 or local state tree laws. It follows natural justice, not the strict Civil Procedure Code, aims to decide within six months , can award compensation and restoration, and its orders can be appealed to the Supreme Court within 90 days.
Strong tribunal or overstretched?

The NGT has acted on the Ganga, Yamuna, Delhi air quality and illegal mining. Critics point to its limited jurisdiction, vacancies, weak execution, and a Supreme Court ruling that it also has some suo motu power (2021). Executive influence over appointments and the narrow list of Acts are a regular concern.
Rights and climate

In M.K. Ranjitsinh v Union of India (2024) the Supreme Court recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change as part of Articles 14 and 21. Local bodies have a role under the 11th Schedule (Article 243G). States also have their own pollution control boards under the Water and Air Acts.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Assess the role of the NGT in environmental governance. What are its limitations?” Structure: origin; jurisdiction; principles; notable orders; limits (narrow Acts, enforcement, vacancies); reforms. Mains-style: “Polluter pays and precautionary principles: how have Indian courts used them?” Prelims tip: NGT Act 2010; Article 48A (42nd Amendment); EPA 1986 after Bhopal; NGT excludes the Wildlife Act.
EIA and Environmental Clearance
The gate every big project must pass

Mines, dams, highways and industries need environmental clearance. EIA stories reach the headlines often: Great Nicobar, Hasdeo, Char Dham. UPSC asks the process, the authorities and the criticism. Remember the 2006 rules, the categories and the stages. EIA is also asked through current cases. The Great Nicobar project, Hasdeo Arand coal mining and Char Dham road widening raised issues of forest clearance, tribal rights and cumulative impact. Answers should name the stages, the authorities (EAC, SEIAA) and one criticism. Also remember that the process is not a veto: a project can be approved with conditions.
What EIA is

Environmental Impact Assessment studies the likely effects of a project before it starts, then proposes measures to avoid or reduce harm. It is a planning tool and a legal requirement. India’s first EIA rules came in 1994 under the Environment Protection Act 1986. They were replaced by the EIA Notification 2006 , which is still the base. The 2006 notification makes prior environmental clearance mandatory for listed projects. Category A projects are appraised at the national level by the Expert Appraisal Committee of the Ministry. Category B projects go to the State Environment Impact Assessment Authority with its State committee. Category B is split into B1, which needs a full EIA, and B2, which does not.
A and B

Projects listed in the schedule are Category A (large, appraised by the Centre’s Expert Appraisal Committee, EAC ) or Category B (appraised by the State’s SEIAA with a State Expert Appraisal Committee). Category B splits into B1 (needs an EIA report) and B2 (no EIA report). Examples: large mining, thermal power, river valley projects, highways above a size, and chemical plants.
Screening to decision

Screening decides if EIA is needed (for B). Scoping fixes the terms of reference. Public consultation has a public hearing at the project site and written comments. The appraisal committee reviews the final report. The authority then grants or rejects, with conditions. After clearance, monitoring and compliance reports follow. Clearance has a set validity.
More than one gate

A project may also need forest clearance (Van Adhiniyam), wildlife board clearance for protected areas, CRZ clearance and consent to establish and operate from the State Pollution Control Board. The PARIVESH portal (2018) puts these online. Ecologically sensitive zones around protected areas add another layer. The Supreme Court in 2022 asked for a 1 km buffer around parks, then modified the order in 2023.
The 2020 draft and ex post facto clearance

The draft EIA 2020 proposed exemptions, shorter hearing notice and post-facto approval for violators. It drew large protests and was not finalised. In Vanashakti v Union of India (2025) the Supreme Court struck down ex post facto environmental clearances; the Court recalled it in November 2025 by 2:1, and a fresh review bench heard the matter in 2026.
Where citizens speak

The hearing is held near the site after a 30-day notice in local languages and newspapers. The State Pollution Control Board runs it with the district collector. The draft EIA report and summary must be available to the public. People can also send written comments. Some projects are exempt from the hearing, such as certain modernisation, defence and border road projects. Critics say language barriers and intimidation weaken the process. Communities have used Gram Sabha resolutions to resist projects, as at Niyamgiri.
Rubber stamp or real check?

Critics say EIA reports are written by hired consultants, hearings are manipulated, cumulative impact is ignored, and post-clearance monitoring is weak. Rejections are rare. Industry says delays raise costs. The balance between speed and safeguards is a standard Mains argument. EIA reports are paid for by the project proponent, so critics say they are biased. Public hearings take place at the project site, but notice periods are short and local people often lack access to the full report. Cumulative impact of many projects in one basin is rarely assessed. Monitoring after clearance depends on self-reported compliance by the proponent, and violations are often regularised through ex post facto clearance.
Landscape-level reports

The Gadgil Committee (WGEEP, 2011) proposed making the whole Western Ghats ecologically sensitive in three zones. The Kasturirangan Committee (2013) kept about 37 percent of the area (around 60,000 sq km) as an ecologically sensitive area. States opposed both in part. Disasters like the Wayanad landslides (2024) revived the debate. The Gadgil panel recommended three zones, banned mining in the most sensitive one, and gave gram sabhas a bottom-up role. The Kasturirangan panel separated cultural landscape from natural landscape and proposed to ban mining, quarrying, sand mining and red-category industries in the sensitive area. The Western Ghats span six states: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
How to answer

Mains-style: “What are the shortcomings of the EIA process in India? Suggest reforms.” Structure: process; flaws (consultant quality, weak hearings, no cumulative assessment, poor monitoring, post-facto approvals); reforms (independent EIA agency, public data, strict compliance). Mains-style: “Gadgil versus Kasturirangan: which approach suits the Western Ghats?” Prelims tip: EIA 1994, replaced 2006. Category A is Central EAC. Category B is State SEIAA. PARIVESH is the clearance portal.
Environmental Movements and Judicial Activism
People and courts shaped the green agenda

Chipko, Appiko, Narmada, Silent Valley and the cases of M.C. Mehta and Godavarman are core GS-I and GS-III material. UPSC asks who, where, when and what changed. These stories show that Indian environmentalism often grew from livelihood, not only from nature love. The movements fall into categories: forest protection (Bishnoi, Chipko, Appiko), displacement from dams (Narmada Bachao Andolan, Silent Valley), and conservation of rights. The judiciary then widened the meaning of Article 21 through public interest litigation. Learn the leader, place, year and result for each, since UPSC asks these as one-line matches in Prelims and as examples in Mains.
Bishnoi and Chipko

Bishnoi (1730) : Amrita Devi and villagers of Khejarli (Jodhpur) died hugging khejri trees. Chipko (1973) : began in Chamoli, Uttarakhand, led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt (Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh) and made famous by Sunderlal Bahuguna . Gaura Devi led women at Reni (1974). It stopped commercial felling in Himalayan forests and led to a 1980 ban on green felling above 1,000 m in the Himalaya. The Bishnoi tradition rests on 29 rules attributed to Guru Jambheshwar. Chipko used non-violent, Gandhian methods led largely by women, so it is also seen as an ecofeminist movement. Its slogan was that ecology is permanent economy. Bahuguna's Himalayan march of 1981 to 1983 ran from Kashmir to Kohima. Appiko (1983) in Karnataka's Western Ghats was inspired by Chipko.
Hug the tree, southern style

Appiko (1983) in Uttara Kannada, Karnataka, led by Pandurang Hegde , used the same tactic in the Western Ghats. Jungle Bachao Andolan (Singhbhum, 1982) opposed teak replacing sal. Silent Valley (1970s–80s) in Kerala stopped a hydroelectric project on the Kunthipuzha. Scientists and the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad led it. The area became a national park in 1984.
Narmada and Tehri

Narmada Bachao Andolan (1985) led by Medha Patkar opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam over displacement. The Supreme Court in 2000 allowed construction with rehabilitation conditions. Tehri Dam protests (led by Bahuguna) cited seismic risk and displacement. These movements raised the issue of who bears the costs of development.
Navdanya, Niyamgiri, Plachimada

Navdanya (Vandana Shiva, 1987) protects native seeds and opposes biopiracy. At Niyamgiri (Odisha) the Dongria Kondh opposed Vedanta’s bauxite mine; in 2013 the Supreme Court told gram sabhas to decide under the Forest Rights Act, and they rejected it. Plachimada (Kerala) saw protests against Coca-Cola’s groundwater use. More recent: Save Aarey (Mumbai metro car shed) and Hasdeo Arand in Chhattisgarh.
PIL and the green court

Public Interest Litigation widened locus standi . Early case: Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v State of UP (1985) , Dehradun quarrying, a first on ecological balance. M.C. Mehta led to CNG buses in Delhi, the Taj Trapezium order (1996) and Ganga tannery rulings. T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad (1995–) turned a plea on a Nilgiri forest into a long-running continuing mandamus that governs forest law. Lafarge Umiam Mining (2011) set rules for forest clearances in mining.
Other lessons

Mitti Bachao and Save Western Ghats campaigns raised soil and forest issues. Bhopal gas tragedy (2–3 December 1984) led to the Environment Protection Act 1986 and the idea of liability for hazardous industry. Ganga cleaning campaigns , anti-plastic drives, and Save Aarey show that urban movements are now active alongside rural ones.
Activism or overreach?

Supporters say courts filled gaps left by weak agencies and protected the commons. Critics say judges made policy without expertise or democratic accountability, and some orders hurt livelihoods (for example, shutting small industry or evicting forest dwellers). Today the NGT and statutory bodies take much of this load.
Environmentalism of the poor

Ramachandra Guha and Madhav Gadgil describe Indian movements as an “environmentalism of the poor” (a phrase also used by Joan Martinez-Alier), rooted in livelihood conflict over commons. Women had a visible role in Chipko and Appiko, linking to ecofeminism. Chipko won the Right Livelihood Award in 1987 and Bahuguna a Padma Vibhushan.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Discuss the contribution of Chipko and other movements to Indian environmental consciousness.” Structure: origin; leaders; methods (non-violence); outcomes (felling bans, national parks, laws); limits; present relevance. Mains-style: “Judicial activism in environment: is it justified?” Prelims tip: Chipko 1973 (Chamoli); Appiko 1983 (Karnataka); NBA 1985; Silent Valley (Kerala); Bishnoi 1730 (Khejarli).
Sustainable Development, SDGs and Green Economy
The big idea behind all environment policy

Sustainable development is asked in Prelims through dates and conferences and in Mains through trade-off questions: growth versus environment, equity across generations. The Brundtland definition and the SDG basics are must-knows. Questions come in three forms. Prelims asks about a conference or report with year and place. Mains asks for a trade-off, such as whether growth and environment can go together. Essay topics use ideas such as intergenerational equity. A good opening is the Brundtland definition, followed by the three pillars and one Indian example.
Brundtland, 1987

The World Commission on Environment and Development, chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland , released Our Common Future in 1987. It defined sustainable development as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Three pillars: economic, social and environmental . Intergenerational equity and intragenerational equity are the core ideas. Brundtland stressed the needs of the world's poor and the limits set by technology and social organisation. The report led to the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. Critics call the concept vague and say it lets growth continue. Weak sustainability allows natural capital to be replaced by manufactured capital, while strong sustainability does not.
Stockholm to Rio+20

Stockholm 1972 : first UN conference on the human environment; UNEP created. Brundtland 1987 . Rio 1992 (Earth Summit): Agenda 21, Rio Declaration, UNFCCC, CBD, forest principles. Johannesburg 2002 : World Summit on Sustainable Development. Rio+20 2012 : “The Future We Want”; agreed to build SDGs and promote green economy.
Agenda 2030

The 17 Sustainable Development Goals with 169 targets were adopted by the UN General Assembly in September 2015 and run to 2030. They replaced the Millennium Development Goals (2000–15, eight goals). SDGs apply to all countries, are indivisible, and include environment goals: 6 (water), 7 (energy), 11 (cities), 12 (consumption and production), 13 (climate), 14 (life below water) and 15 (life on land).
Measuring and limits

Planetary boundaries (Rockström and others, 2009) give safe limits for nine Earth systems. Doughnut economics (Kate Raworth, 2017) seeks a safe and just space between social floor and ecological ceiling. The Environmental Kuznets Curve claims pollution first rises with income, then falls, but evidence is mixed. Weak sustainability allows manmade capital to replace nature; strong sustainability says natural capital cannot be fully replaced. Ecological footprint and green GDP are measures.
What it means

UNEP’s 2008 Green Economy Initiative defines a green economy as one that improves wellbeing and equity while reducing environmental risk. It includes renewable energy, circular economy, green jobs and nature-based solutions. Critics say “green growth” hides continued resource use, and that poor countries need room to grow (degrowth debate).
Equity in action

India’s negotiating line at Rio and since is common but differentiated responsibilities : rich countries caused most historic emissions and must lead. Rio Principle 7 gives this its basis. At home, Article 48A and 51A(g) , along with the Environment Protection Act 1986 , give the legal base. India’s Voluntary National Reviews report SDG progress to the UN.
Growth versus environment

Developing countries argue that development is the first need and that rich countries must lead. Others say the poor suffer most from degradation. The idea of just transition tries to link both. The question also divides carbon prices, subsidies and trade rules. The Environmental Kuznets Curve idea holds that pollution rises with income and then falls, but critics say this is not automatic. Developing countries point to the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, since rich countries emitted more in the past. Just transition means that workers and regions that depend on coal or other polluting activity are supported, not abandoned, when policy changes.
India and the SDGs

NITI Aayog publishes the SDG India Index. Its 2023–24 edition (released 2025) reported a national composite score of about 71, up from 66 in 2020–21 (as of 2025). Schemes such as GOBARdhan (2018), Jal Jeevan Mission , Ujjwala and Swachh Bharat map onto goals. India’s Green Growth is one of the seven priorities of Budget 2023–24. India’s Mission LiFE and the 2070 net-zero target tie in. The SDG India Index ranks states and Union Territories using indicators on poverty, health and clean energy, and Kerala has often ranked among the top states. It supports cooperative federalism by making states compete. The National Indicator Framework is run by MoSPI, and localisation of SDGs takes goals down to panchayats.
How to answer

Mains-style: “Sustainable development is a balancing act. Examine how India can balance growth and environment.” Structure: definition; three pillars; Indian pressures (poverty, energy, population); tools (EIA, renewables, SDG localisation, green finance); conclusion with equity. Prelims tip: Brundtland 1987. SDGs 2015: 17 goals, 169 targets. Agenda 21 from Rio 1992. UNEP created after Stockholm 1972.
Sustainable Agriculture and Biotechnology Concerns
Food security without ecological collapse

The Green Revolution fed India but drained groundwater, loaded soils with chemicals and cut diversity. Natural farming and GM crops are both in the news, and UPSC asks for balanced views. This lesson covers the farm-side answer and the biotech debate. The Green Revolution of the 1960s raised wheat and rice output through high-yielding varieties, fertiliser and irrigation, but it also caused falling water tables in Punjab and Haryana, soil degradation and heavy chemical use. Biotechnology is offered as both a solution, with higher yields and fewer sprays, and a risk. UPSC expects a balanced view with evidence.
What sustainable agriculture means

It aims to produce enough food while protecting soil, water and biodiversity and keeping farmers’ incomes stable. Methods: organic farming , integrated pest management , crop rotation, conservation agriculture, drip irrigation, agroforestry, System of Rice Intensification . Related ideas: agroecology, climate-smart agriculture and regenerative practices. Sikkim became India's first fully organic state in 2016. The Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (2015) supports organic clusters, and natural farming has been promoted in Andhra Pradesh. IPM uses biological control, pheromone traps and resistant varieties to cut pesticide use. SRI saves water and seed by planting young single seedlings widely spaced.
Natural and organic farming

Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (2015) promotes organic clusters. Sikkim became India’s first fully organic state in 2016. The National Mission on Natural Farming (approved November 2024) aims to bring around a crore farmers into chemical-free farming. Soil Health Card (2015), neem-coated urea and PM-PRANAM (2023, to cut chemical fertiliser) support the shift. PMKSY promotes “per drop more crop.”
Millets and water

The UN observed 2023 as the International Year of Millets at India’s initiative. Millets are hardy and need little water, so they suit dry areas. Micro-irrigation saves water and fertiliser. Debate: can organic farming feed India? Sri Lanka’s abrupt 2021 chemical ban, which hurt yields, is often cited as a warning against sudden shifts.
The position in India

Bt cotton (approved 2002) is the only GM crop in commercial cultivation in India. The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) under the Environment Protection Act (Rules 1989) approves GM releases. Bt brinjal was put under a moratorium in 2010 by Environment Minister Jairam Ramesh. GM mustard (DMH-11) was cleared by GEAC in October 2022; the Supreme Court gave a split verdict in July 2024 and asked the Centre to frame a national GM policy.
A newer route

In 2022 the Centre exempted certain genome-edited plants (SDN-1 and SDN-2) without foreign DNA from GM rules. In May 2025, India released two genome-edited rice varieties developed by ICAR institutes. Supporters say this is faster and safer than transgenics. Critics seek tight oversight and labelling.
Why people worry

Gene flow to wild relatives and loss of crop diversity. Pest resistance (pink bollworm in Bt cotton). Corporate control of seeds and high prices; fears over terminator seeds (GURTs), which are not allowed. Health and allergen questions; labelling. Unapproved herbicide-tolerant cotton spreading illegally. Pink bollworm resistance to Bt cotton became visible in Gujarat and other states, forcing farmers to use more pesticide. Terminator technology, GURTs, makes seeds sterile so that farmers must buy fresh seed each year, which is banned in India. Labelling of GM food is regulated by FSSAI. Illegal herbicide-tolerant cotton shows weak enforcement of biosafety rules.
Seeds and knowledge

The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act 2001 protects breeders and farmers’ right to save and sell seeds. The Biological Diversity Act 2002 controls access to biological resources and fights biopiracy (cases: neem, turmeric, basmati). The Cartagena Protocol (2000) governs biosafety of GMOs. Geographical Indications protect traditional products. The PPV&FR Act lets a farmer register a variety and rewards communities, with an authority and a Gene Fund. The Biological Diversity Act 2002 created the National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai), State Biodiversity Boards and local Biodiversity Management Committees. Benefit sharing follows the Nagoya Protocol (2010) under the CBD. Basmati and Darjeeling tea carry GI tags.
Balanced view

Biotech can raise yields, cut pesticide use and add nutrition (golden rice, biofortified crops). Risks include corporate dominance and unknown long-term effects. Many experts want case-by-case approval, independent testing and public data. A sustainable path can use both: agroecology as the base and tested biotech as a tool.
How to answer

Mains-style: “GM crops: a boon or a bane for Indian agriculture? Discuss.” Structure: status (Bt cotton only); benefits; concerns; regulation (GEAC, Cartagena); court position (GM mustard 2024); way forward (transparent science, gene-editing rules, farmer choice). Mains-style: “How can natural farming help achieve sustainable agriculture in India?” Prelims tip: Bt cotton 2002; Bt brinjal moratorium 2010; GEAC under EPA; Sikkim organic 2016; Cartagena = biosafety.
